speechtext: The House resumed from Thursday, October 10, consideration of the motion of Mrs. McDougall that Bill C-79, an Act respecting the provision of compensation to depositors of Canadian Commercial Bank, CCB Mortgage Investment Corporation and Northland Bank in respect of uninsured deposits, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee; and the amendment of Mr. Turner (Vancouver Quadra) (p. 7379).
Mr. Speaker, it is both with pleasure and with a sense of dismay that one has to speak this morning on this Bill.
Is it a pleasurable dismay?

It is a pleasure to be able to convey to the House the sense of sadness one has to feel because this Bill has been brought before the House by the Government.
This Bill represents a story of corporate irresponsibility on the part of a bank but it also represents a story of Government mismanagement with respect to the handling of this entire affair. The level of corporate irresponsibility has become quite clear as the testimony of Mr. Hitchman has proceeded in the Estey inquiry. We find that this former banker, who has had the opportunity to actually dig into the details of this operation, has uncovered an incredible mare's nest. The operation of this bank was simply not acceptable and Mr. Hitchman suggests that that fact could have been easily discerned if somebody had taken the time to investigate the matter with care back in March. His report demonstrates not just the corporate irresponsibility of the bank but the sense of mismanagement which has been demonstrated by the Government in carrying this bail-out procedure forward, beginning in March.
I think we have to speak with sadness about the willingness of the Government to commit what is now $875 million for these two banks despite the lack of detailed information back in March which Mr. Hitchman has said could clearly have been available.
What we have is not just a story of Government mismanagement and corporate irresponsibility. It is also a story which characterizes the misplaced priorities of this Government. As I look at this Bill and the huge sums of money that are going to be spent because of it, I have to think of the farmers of Essex county on whose behalf I had to write to the Farm Credit Corporation and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) this past winter pointing out that the farmers were going to lose their farms because of the lack of special government help for the farm community. The answer we received was, "We cannot afford to help those farmers".
As well, I have to think of a small, struggling company based in my constituency called Diversified Fuel Components which had to try source after source to receive assistance in getting through a difficult financial period. Ultimately this company did get such help, but it received it from the provincial Government, not the federal Government, despite the fact that programs should have been available to help this kind of innovative firm. Yet the answer that that company received in response to request after request I raised on its behalf was that there simply is not enough money available.
I have to think of older workers who are in their late fifties and had worked for companies like Champion Spark Plug which again is situated in my constituency. These workers had been part of an enterprise which, from 1978 to 1984, had been able to get assistance under the Labour Adjustment Benefits Program. When these workers were laid off this past summer, they made a simple request. Like their counterparts who had received help up until February 1984, they too as older workers wanted to receive help with the very difficult problems faced by older workers who are unemployed. Yet once more, the answer that came back to me from the Minister of Labour (Mr. McKnight) was, "I am sorry, we do not have enough money".
I have to think of the people of Essex-Windsor who want assistance for the Hiatus House which provides assistance to women who are caught up in the transition between marriage and independence. Many women have to leave their family homes and they face great difficulties in doing so. Hiatus House, supported mostly by private charities from the Windsor and Essex county areas, provides help for them to make that transition. Not only for Hiatus House but for transition houses like it across the country, we have requested that help be made available. That was one of the recommendations of our action group report on jobs which we wrote this past winter. Once more, the answer that came back to us was, "We do not have the money for that kind of thing".

I have to think of construction companies within my constituency which requested that the increase in sales tax that would hit those small producers be postponed for a year to permit them to phase it into their contracts, a quite straightforward and reasonable request. Once more the answer came back from the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson): "We do not have the money." Thus, we end up with farmers, small business people, older workers, women, and medium-sized construction companies saying to the Government: "Look, here are sensible matters which need just a little bit of money", and the Government comes back with the answer: "No. We do not have that type of financing available."
Then we saw two banks get into trouble, and suddenly $875 million was made available. It is not available for poor individuals, hard pressed widows or desperate credit unions, but, as the statistics made clear, it is available for foreign banks, other Canadian banks, investment dealers, large Canadian corporations and life insurance companies which will receive the majority of the support which this Bill is to provide.
To conclude, I think this is an immoral, irresponsible Bill which reveals far too clearly that the priorities of the Government lie with the rich and the wealthy as opposed to the poor, the weak, the hard pressed-the people who can make a contribution to the future of our economy.

Mr. Speaker, I wish I could say that I am pleased to participate in the debate this morning. However, I am not.
For the first time in over 50 years a bank folded in September of this year. Only a few weeks later a second bank found itself in a similar predicament. This is as a result of a Government which, last summer, made campaign speeches across the land saying to the people of Canada: "Vote for us. We are business-like. We can run the country in a businesslike manner. We are friends of business and banks which can really associate with us. We can do things more productively". That is what the Tories said last summer. What happened to their business-like manner in running the country? If this is business-like I wonder what type of business those Hon. Members across the way were in before they were elected to the House. I certainly hope they were not running those businesses the way they are running the country because we would be in even deeper trouble if the businesses of the country were run as badly as this Government is run. Of course, the Government says, as did the Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDou-gall): "It is not our fault. It is the fault of the previous Government". That is what the Minister of State for Finance said in the House. She said: "Blame it on the previous administration. Blame everything on the previous administration".
Hear, hear!
There is one of those generic Tories, Mr. Speaker. He is one of those Members from whom we very seldom hear.
It's better than being a Taiwan Liberal.

Here is someone who very seldom speaks in the House and who is now saying: "Hear, hear".
Let me bring to your attention, Mr. Speaker, the Hitchman Report which was commissioned on June 25 by the Minister of State for Finance and which was tabled on August 12. Whose fault is it, according to Mr. Hitchman? He does not talk about the National Energy Program or all of those other reasons given by the Minister of State for Finance.
He is a Liberal.
An Hon. Member across the way says that His Honour the Judge is a Liberal.
Who appointed him?
He was appointed by the Tories. He is a well qualified-

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. 1 am glad you brought the Hon. Member for Ontario (Mr. Fennell) into line. He certainly needs it.
I was just going to read from the report of George Hitchman. What does it state as reasons for the failure of the bank? He said that of the 84 loan accounts he reviewed, he found that 28 of those had no financial statements; 11 had financial statements which were over a year old; and 45 had financial statements but some of them lacked sufficient detail in order to assess the loan properly. This is the way in which the banks, which were supervised by the Government, were run. This is the kind of administration we have.
October 22, 1985

I have an article from The Toronto Star dated October 22 in my hand. The article is entitled, "Expert assails poor records of failed bank". It states in part, and I quote:
Retired banker George Hitchman reiterated his report's conclusions before a federal inquiry that the Edmonton bank's management had engaged in unsound banking practices and kept poor records of the bank's affairs.
I hope that clears up the Minister's erroneous and sometimes misleading comments. She has accused previous administrations of these failures, but these are Tory failures. They are nothing else but Tory failures caused by a bad Government.
We know, Mr. Speaker, that in a very few days there will be additional tax measures which will be implemented as a result of the disastrous Budget of last May 23. We know, of course, that those tax increases will total $2.6 billion. What is interesting is that if one adds the cost of the Gulf fiasco and the cost of the bank bail-outs, one finds that the total comes to just about the identical amount. So the blunders of this Government over the last three months have cost the taxpayers the same amount as the tax increase which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) is inflicting or will be inflicting on the people of Canada over the next few months. There is no excuse for this kind of administration.
I would like to read to you, Mr. Speaker, what some of the farmers in my riding think of the priorities of this Government in bailing out banks versus helping out the needy. I would like to read a letter which is signed by Lorraine and Richard Lapointe of Martintown, Ontario, in the riding of Stormont, Dundas, which is temporarily held by a Conservative Member. The letter says:
Dear Mr. Warner:
At a time when your Government is cutting back on Agricultural programs and planning to phase out subsidy payments to dairy farmers, it is disappointing and frustrating to see you so eager to reimburse the depositors of a failed bank.
Investors knew there was a risk involved and were fully aware of the insurance limitations.
NOW TELL US WHY ALL CANADIANS HAVE TO PAY!
A copy of that letter went to the Minister of Finance. I want the record to show that a Member to my right says that these people are my cousins. I am sure Mr. and Mrs. Lapointe of the riding of Stormont-Dundas will take that accusation for what it is worth. If they voted Tory in the past, the Tories just lost two votes. We know they have none to spare and they have lost two more because of partisan remarks such as the Hon. Member just made against the good people of Stormont-Dundas.
This is the situation we are facing in this country. We have a Government which does not want to give any priority to the concerns and problems of the farmer. We have a Government which is failing to live up to the campaign promises it made to the good people of Canada last summer.

I see the Secretary of State agrees with what I just said since he nodded his approval. I invite him to cross the floor

and join us. He is starting to see the light, a bit late, perhaps, but it is never too late for a Conservative to let himself be inspired by ideas that make more sense than that party's philosophy, Mr. Speaker.
In any case, it is clear the Government is making a mistake by wanting, to reimburse depositors in this way, that is, without letting the House and the people of Canada know where the money is going to.

Why can the people of Canada not be told who this money is going to, Mr. Speaker? Finally, how did the Minister of State for Finance decide that certain investors were going to be reimbursed and certain investors were not? In my view, people who deposited in excess of $60,000 in these banks are clearly investors just like anyone else. Why are they reimbursed and the preferred shareholders, for instance, not reimbursed? What is the difference? They are both investors. They have both invested money which is uninsured. One is being assisted and one is not. This is unfair and the Government should really rethink this whole measure in order to improve it.

Mr. Speaker, it is clear today, as it has been for some time, that this debate should end. It has become repetitive and unproductive, and nothing has shown that more than the two opposition speeches delivered today. The NDP has shown today, as it has previously in this debate, that the only new thing it has is the word "New" in its name. In this debate the NDP has dragged into this Chamber every tired-out, used up idea, cliche and trite saying which it has been storing up, saving, cherishing, indeed revering, since the Regina Manifesto. However, they all add up to one thing: That Party is against banks, business and anything which builds up the economy and causes this country to prosper.
We are against Tories.

With a fine disdain for the truth NDP Members seized on one feature of the Bill, the possibility that it will be helping foreign banks. The thought that some of our resources could go to foreign banks has really gripped their imagination. They have implied to the public that that is what the Bill is all about even though the facts show that only 12 per cent of the money involved is going to foreign banks. Where does the other 88 per cent go? This is something that has received no attention from the NDP at all. For example, the compensation of the credit unions will amount to 14 per cent, more than that of the foreign banks. Does the NDP want those credit unions to be bereft as a result of these banks ending their days? The compensation for the provinces and municipalities will total 21 per cent of the funds involved. Does the NDP want the western provinces to be ignored? Would it want those provincial Governments and municipalities to be left behind? I should not want to think that the NDP Members are that indifferent to the well-being of the provinces and municipalities of western Canada and other regions, but that certainly could be inferred from the addresses they have given.

What about the labour unions and the religious organizations? What about the universities? There is a cause. It being National Universities Week this week, the Opposition has reminded us that the Government should be providing more. If the Opposition had its way, we would ignore the needs of universities, religious organizations and labour unions that had money on deposit in these banks.
With regard to the Liberals, Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that they should have stayed out of this debate altogether. They have clearly been part of the problem rather than the solution. Their finance critic, the Hon. Member for Trinity (Miss Nicholson), for whom I have high regard, made the point in her address early in the debate that no bank has ever failed during a Liberal administration. I had thought that we had a bank failure in the early 1920s during the King administration. However, that is a historical point which may have been passed by. The point which we must focus on is one in more recent history which is familiar even to members of the Liberal caucus, namely, that under their administration the banking system was allowed to expand from 11 institutions to 70, while the staff of the Inspector General of Banks was kept static at eight inspectors. That fact could not be ignored, even by their finance critic, who said:
I do not know why additional staff was not added to the office of the Inspector General of Banks at a time when, following the revision of the Bank Act, the number of banks in Canada was greatly increased. There was a rather obvious case to be made for increasing the number of inspectors.
It was obvious to everyone but the Liberal Government in office at the time. The Liberals have been part of the problem and now they are trying to be part of the solution.

The "fatuous forty" in this debate have marched in day after day and emptied themselves as though the people of Canada had rejected them not only in 1984, but a year later, in September, 1985, have done precisely the same thing again. I note that the Liberals have been feeling much better in the past several weeks. Due to Question Period they were sure that they were on their way back. However, just last week the Gallup poll showed that in September-

One could say of this that when all they get is 29, all they can do is yearn and pine. In fact we can go on to say that come '88 they'll still have to wait. The fact is, Mr. Speaker, that under the administration of this Government the economy has turned around. The reason for that is that there has been confidence restored in the possibilities for doing business in this country.

speechtext: Busted banks, rotten fish.

This Bill is itself a confidence builder. It is directed toward that objective because it is a way in which the Government demonstrates its commitment to keep the pledge that was implied, if not articulated, in asking the depositors in these banks to continue depositing.
It should be clear to us all, Mr. Speaker, that business prospers when there is confidence among those doing business, one with another. Indeed, so much of our business today depends upon that kind of mutual trust. An investor has to be amazed at the way in which the securities industry of this country day by day depends upon people being able to rely upon the commitments that one makes to another. Without that reliance the whole thing would collapse. If you found that commitments which were made were not honoured, at the very least you would not do business with that person again.
This is an example in which the Government asked people to leave their money on deposit in two banks that were in trouble. In the interest of the country as a whole, but particularly in the economy of the western region, the Government was trying to assist, stabilize, and help these banks to survive. When that was no longer possible and it became clear that in spite of that assistance those institutions were no longer viable, the Government made the kind of hard decision which Governments sometimes have to make and decided that those banks would have to be allowed to close their doors. Having made that decision, and having earlier made a commitment to those depositors, institutions and individuals alike, it was right that the Government keep its word, articulated and implied, to depositors, who responded to its request and, at considerable risk to themselves, made an impressive effort to keep the banks alive.
That was not a bail-out like the bail-out of Maislin Transport in Montreal under the former administration. No shareholders of this bank were bailed out. Those shareholders had to bear the risk. No Government came to their rescue. The only assistance given by this Bill is to those depositors who put their money at risk and made it possible for those banks to continue operations during the time that they did.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, we consider this Bill to be appropriate to the general effort that has been made by the Government to restore business confidence and to renew the economy. I think it will be clear from the passage of this Bill that the business community knows it can count on the word of the Government.

Mr. Speaker, I am happy to join in this debate because I think that the Hon. Member for
October 22, 1985

Scarborough West (Mr. Stackhouse) has just displayed his great ignorance of what we are debating here. We are debating a reasoned amendment by the Hon. Member for Vancouver Quadra, the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner). That amendment reads:
That the motion be amended by deleting all the words after the word "That" and substituting the following therefore:
"this House declines to give second reading to a Bill, the principle of which is to permit payments of large, but unspecified amounts of public monies to unspecified persons or corporations, thereby substantially denegrating Parliamentary accountability for expenditure of public funds".
Surely, Mr. Speaker, the very basis of parliamentary democracy and our accountability is the bringing of the Estimates of various Departments of the Government before the House or before a parliamentary committee in order to determine exactly what the expenditures are for. The Government is asking for a blank cheque. It is saying that it will not give any details about who the money is being paid to. Is it to their Tory friends in Alberta? We do not know; maybe it is not. We should know if it is.
Surely it is basic to parliamentary democracy to know who will be receiving the money, whether it is their bank friends in Toronto or California or anyone else. We should be entitled to more detail either from the Estey Commission or the parliamentary committee.
When we get to the committee stage of this Bill I hope we will be able to find out the names of those with the hundreds and thousands of dollars in bad loans. We should also know that information because this whole episode really speaks of a political fix.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) made an incredible decision on the spur of the moment to bail out a bank. He made his Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDougall) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) agree with this decision even when they, in their own incompetence, realized it was a terrible mistake. However, when the Prime Minister made this decision over a weekend, those Ministers did not advise the Prime Minister to have an audit conducted by the senior banks who participated in the bail-out. Those banks were also pressured by the Prime Minister to invest millions of dollars in that bail-out. I suggest this is the worst fiasco in Canadian banking history.
A very interesting article in The Financial Post has the headline, "Never-ending circle of passing the buck". This article outlines how the $1.3 billion worth Canadian Commercial Bank fiasco takes place. First, the Minister of State for Finance and the Minister of Finance cannot be faulted because they did not attend the meeting. Although the bankers, the Deputy Minister of Finance and the Inspector General of Banks attended the meeting, it is amazing that the Minister of State for Finance and the Minister of Finance did not attend that meeting where a decision is made to put up $255 million. Since those Ministers cannot be responsible for such a decision if they did not attend the meeting, that is how the buck is passed in that circumstance.

The Governor of the Bank of Canada stated that he had no direct knowledge of the state of the bank's finances. It is amazing that he would advance hundreds of millions of dollars when he does not bother to check and does not know anything about the state of the finances. He stated, "The Bank of Canada is not involved in monitoring the Financial soundness of individual banks and supervising their behaviour". Therefore, the buck is passed again because he is not responsible. Who is in charge if it is not the Governor of the Bank of Canada? What about the Inspector General of Banks, Mr. Kennett? The article states:
No, not his fault either, if you listen to the rumours. He and former Deputy Minister of Finance Mickey Cohen, you see, actually argued against the bail-out.
Therefore, they are not responsible. They are said to have been overruled by the Government Ministers. Of course, they are not responsible because they were not at the meeting. It is a perfect circle of buck-passing.
I believe the responsibility lies with the Prime Minister. Obviously he made the decision and, incredibly, his Ministers knuckled under and agreed to it. However, a three-day audit would have given sufficient warning to these Ministers to advise the Prime Minister that this bail-out was a useless exercise. This view was stated by the consultant at yesterday's hearings.
The Hon. Member for Scarborough West stated that confidence has been restored. However, I would ask him, in what area this confidence has been restored? The $60 million requested by the Government last March will ultimately cost the Government a billion dollars. This certainly did not restore confidence in investors in the Northland Bank because that bank has failed. It has not restored confidence in depositors in the Mercantile Bank because it faced a terrible run on its deposits.
I suggest that the Hon. Member is doing a lot of wishful thinking if he believes confidence has been restored in these areas. Small banks like the Bank of British Columbia as well as the Continental Bank have had to raise interest rates in the face of serious problems. Therefore, rather than renewed confidence in the country we have had the greatest lack of confidence in our banking system in 62 years. Two banks have failed and another bank had such a serious run on its deposits that it had to amalgamate with another bank.
The Government should have investigated the matter and conducted the proper audits rather than acting on the Prime Minister's quick political judgment. The Northland Bank would probably be in business today and the Government would have saved hundreds of millions of dollars. Therefore, 1 believe the Government should accept our amendment which states that:
this House declines to give second reading to a Bill, the principle of which is to permit payments of large, but unspecified amounts of public monies to unspecified persons or corporations, thereby substantially denigrating Parliamentary accountability for expenditure of public funds.
If we do not accept such an amendment, hundreds of millions of dollars will be spent without any information as to

who will receive these moneys and why they are being paid out in this irresponsible way.

Mr. Speaker, the amendment before us today is a reasoned motion. Rather than paying the $875 million to uninsured depositors in the Northland Bank and Canadian Commercial Bank, the amendment states:
this House declines to give second reading to a Bill, the principle of which is to permit payments of large, but unspecified amounts of public monies to unspecified persons or corporations, thereby substantially denigrating Parliamentary accountability for expenditure of public funds.
This is an extremely important principle. The main reason for the existence of Parliament is to oversee the expenditure of parliamentary funds and to approve taxation measures which the Government, of formerly the Monarch, decided upon or proposed. This is the very essence of why we are here as Members of Parliament. We are looking at a proposal which will pay out some $875 million in a bail-out package to the uninsured depositors of those two banks. If we are to be credible parliamentarians, we should look at the background of the situation to see the legal requirement for the country to make such an expenditure. It does not take very much searching. There is no legal requirement to do that. In fact, that is what the entire Bill is about; it is trying to create the legal framework whereby Parliament and the country will guarantee $875 million to the uninsured depositors of those banks. It is a fundamental change of the laws.
With all deference to the Hon. Member for Scarborough West (Mr. Stackhouse) who is now out of the Chamber but perhaps is listening, I do not think there were any previous examples of this happening in the country. He cited Maislin trucking in Quebec when the Liberal Government bailed out its shareholders. He said that this case was not like that because we were not bailing out the shareholders of the two banks. If he had understood the situation, or perhaps had been more honest with us, he would have recognized what he was doing by supporting a Bill to bail out shareholders to a total of $875 million in uninsured deposits. This particular Bill makes certain that in essence the shareholders of the Northland Bank and the Canadian Commercial Bank receive another $875 million when the final computations are made as to the worth of the remaining assets of the two banks. It increases the value of those assets because the money held by shareholders in shares will not be reduced to pay off part of the liabilities of uninsured shareholders. It becomes a zero liability against the two banks and therefore leaves far more in the pot for the two bankrupt companies to redistribute to the original shareholders. In fact, it is a bail-out of the shareholders of those two banks in a more indirect way than perhaps the Hon. Member understood. In essence, it puts another $875 million to $900 million into the pool of assets to be redistributed to shareholders.
Who are the people who will benefit from the pay-out? This is the crux of the debate for the last number of days. The list which was presented to us was prepared by the Ministry. It
does not tell us who will be the beneficiaries of this $875 million. The Government hides behind a section in the Bank Act and says that that kind of information cannot be made available. However, when one looks at the Acts relating to bankruptcy, those laws require that individuals or corporations that wish to participate in receiving funds from a dismantled company due to bankruptcy must come forward to make public their names and get on the list in order to share in the division of the bankrupt's property. That is not being required in this case, simply because the Government chooses to look at the Bank Act rather than at the Acts relating to bankruptcy.
Whom is it bailing out? We do not know the individuals. We know them by categories. According to the information provided to us, just barely 2 per cent of the money from the $875 million bail-out will find its way into the pockets of individuals. Most of the deposits of individuals are covered by the $60,000 for which all depositors are insured when they put money into a financial institution due to the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation.
One thing that has bothered me about this whole proposal is the blinkers worn by Government Members, including Ministers, when they deal with this particular proposition. They fail to see it as denigrating the roles of Members of Parliament and of Parliament itself by taking away the right to know where money goes. On top of that, they hide behind an analysis of the situation which I think is quite faulty. We know from the facts which have been compiled that the Canadian Commercial Bank and the Northland Bank both grew very rapidly in the early 1980s. For instance, the Canadian Commercial Bank saw its assets jump to $3.1 billion in fiscal year 1984 from a mere $864 million in 1980. In a matter of four years, it quadrupled its amount of assets. I remind the House that assets in bank terms mean the money lent out to individuals and other corporations. Northland experienced a similar kind of rapid growth. Its 1984 assets totalled $1.1 billion compared with $254 million in 1980. Northland issued four times as much in the way of loans in a period of four years in the early 1980s.
The Government has tried to make much of the National Energy Program as a contributing factor to the failure of the two banks. I am not sure how that computes, whether the Government means that the oil companies felt so confident in the National Energy Program that they rushed out and borrowed a lot of money, or that somehow the National Energy Program worsened the prospects of oil companies and therefore made them go out to borrow money. In any case, I have trouble following the logic. In March, we had the Western Accord which was supposed to correct all the problems existing in the oil industry. The skies were suddenly looking clear again and, if we listen to the Minister of Energy, everything was looking up in the energy business. Yet, that was the time when it was decided that the loans held by these banks were no longer viable, that they were bad loans. Suddenly these energy companies, despite the new times which are supposed to be coming with the Western Accord, will no longer be good. That tells me that somehow the Western Accord had not improved
October 22, 1985

economic conditions in western Canada and, in fact, it was more prudent to fold up these two banks. The Government recognizes that and therefore has gone ahead and done it.
I do not see where the analysis follows the actions of the Government. I think there is a great deal that the Government is not telling us. We have to have further information before Parliament can legitimately pass this Bill.

Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to join my colleagues in opposing this amendment. I certainly am very pleased to follow my colleague, the Hon. Member for Humboldt-Lake Centre (Mr. Althouse), and to be able to pick up on some of the points he made. We are both from western Canada and I think that there is a western perspective which we must present when speaking of these two banks.
I found it interesting that the Hon. Member for Humboldt-Lake Centre, like many of his NDP colleagues, did not jump up and down and say that we should give money to the credit unions, the unions and the individuals, the very people for whom he supposedly speaks. It seems to me that members of the NDP are trying to make political points on the fact that there are some other banks involved, banks which invested in the two banks that failed. I would like to suggest that ordinary people like ourselves and our constituents invest in banks and buy shares in them. Let us not pretend that banks are almighty corporate beings. They are made up of ordinary people as well. I would like to drive that point home.
I received a letter from a small businessman who had in excess of $100,000 on deposit in one of these banks. He invested not his savings but his cash flow in the bank on a 30-day basis. The collapse of the bank froze his operating capital and he had to lay off his workers. That meant lost jobs. Without additional money, he may not be able to proceed on two committed contracts. This will force him into a breach of contract, a permanent lay-off of workers and possibly a bankruptcy. This businessman is typical of many Canadians who are looking for assistance from Bill C-79. If his business fails, workers in the City of Saskatoon will lose their jobs and it will be because of the Liberals and the NDP Members who are so violently opposing this Bill.
Yesterday I asked this particular contractor if he knew why he had not received his money. He indicated that he did and that he was furious. He was upset with the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Turner) and the Leader of the NDP (Mr. Broadbent) and he has written letters to them to tell them so. I think that is just one example of people who are experiencing difficult times. These people have to pay off their subtrades and their employees and now find themselves in a situation that could very well mean that their small businesses could go under.
The Hon. Member who spoke previously mentioned that big oil companies were making investments back in the days prior to the National Energy Program. I say that the National

Energy Program was not a kick in the shins, it was a kick in the teeth. It meant the virtual collapse of the western Canadian economy. It was not just the big oil companies that were making investments. Small businessmen and individuals were making investments as well. You will understand, Mr. Speaker, coming as you do from Edmonton in the Province of Alberta, that people lost their homes, their cars and their businesses and are now trying to make a comeback as a result of the Western Accord and the good news from the Government indicating that it is prepared to set some rules and live by them, without changing them every time it feels that it is the right thing to do.
I would like to inform the House of things that have happened post NEP as a result of the Western Accord and the Atlantic Accord, particularly from a western perspective. A survey was taken by the Canadian Federation of Independent Businessmen to which there were 10,000 respondents, and it was just released on Thursday or Friday. It gives us some idea of what is beginning to happen across the country and how different it is from the results of tampering with the economy of western Canada that the Liberal Party did back in the late 1970s and early 1980s. One of the questions asked in the survey was, "What are your current plans for investment in your business in the coming six months?" Nationally, 42 per cent of people at the small business sector said that they intend to increase their level of investment. In Saskatchewan alone, that percentage is 36. For businessmen right across the country, this means that people will be going back to work.
The next question was about working capital including inventory. Nationally, 40 per cent of the 10,000 respondents said that they planned to increase their working capital and inventory. In the Province of Saskatchewan that figure was 34 per cent.
The next question was, "In the past six months, has employment in your firm remained the same, increased or decreased?" Nationally, 34 per cent said that it has increased in the past six months.
Some Hon. Members may feel that I am getting off the subject but I do not think I am. That is what this is all about. Those two western Canadian banks got into some very serious difficulty as a result of the National Energy Program. The Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell (Mr. Boudria) can say that the Liberals had nothing to do with that, but I think that the Liberals must certainly take some share of the blame for this particular problem.
Liberal Members are trying to tell us that two banks collapsed as a result of the outcome of the election held on September 4, 1984. I would like to deal with the year 1980 when the Liberal Government expanded the banking system by almost seven times. A great many people in Canada did not argue with that but some did. However, the key point is that the Liberals forgot to do one thing. They forgot to make adjustments and update the regulatory system of the banks. When Liberal Members point their Fingers at the management of the banks-and I am not saying that these banks were perfect-I suggest that they take a look at their own back

yards and realize that they should have looked at the regulatory system of the banks. This is where I must salute the Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDougall) who has begun this long overdue process.
As the Hon. Member for Humboldt-Lake Centre just mentioned, there has been much discussion about releasing the names of the depositors. I wonder how the Hon. Member for Humboldt-Lake Centre would feel if the Bank of Canada made his private financial statements available to the rest of the country. I say that that is private information. In one of the major financial newspapers, the headline for this morning reads, "Estey unlikely to release names of bank depositors," and I say, rightly so. I find it difficult to understand how members of the Liberal Party and the NDP who oppose modification of indexation on the grounds that it will hurt ordinary Canadians can publicly oppose a Bill that will save the livelihoods of thousands of people in every one of our constituencies. Again, I am talking particularly of those in western Canada. People who live in western Canada made investment decisions on the basis of what they knew at the time. At one time there was a buoyant economy in the West because of activity in the energy sector, the engine of growth in western Canada. People who made investment decisions on that basis had every right to believe that the economy would remain buoyant. I think opposition Members have to take a good, hard look at this particular issue from a western perspective and realize that there are thousands of people who are stranded and need assistance. For every day that we delay this Bill, it is costing us more and more in interest.

Mr. Speaker, it gives me a great deal of pleasure to be able to speak on the amendment and say how pleased I am with the position taken by the Liberal Party in declining to give second reading to Bill C-79. The principle of this Bill is to permit large but unspecified amounts of public moneys to go to unspecified persons or corporations, thereby denigrating parliamentary accountability for expenditure of public funds.
This is a very large sum of money that the Government is proposing to give to the depositors of two western banks.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Uninsured.

Depositors over $60,000 are completely uninsured. The Government is speaking of $875 million. I personally believe that the amount that it will cost the Government and the taxpayers of Canada is substantially more than that. How did this situation arise? Why is the Government in this position? Why has so much damage been done to the banking system, to the depositors of these banks and to the
taxpayers of this country? Why, when the Government decided to investigate this question in March of 1985 and formed the bail-out group, did this bail-out group rely only on information that the Canadian Commercial Bank itself chose to make available to them? Why would the Government rely on information that the bank in question was choosing to making available?
On March 22, 1985, the officers seconded from the Royal Bank of Canada reported that they could not accurately assess the effectiveness of the support package because they had not had full access to the books. This is incredible.
The Hon. Member for Saskatoon East (Mr. Ravis) is saying that it is the fault of the previous Liberal Government that the inspection process of the bank is not better than it is today. I agree that it should be tighter. I agree that is should have been done before, but this Government has been in power for over a year and now it is just coming to grips with the question. How long is it going to take it to improve the inspection service in this country? Do banks have to fail before any action is taken? Is this what the Government does, wait for the catastrophes to happen before it puts into place the action that is necessary to correct these situations and, hopefully, to prohibit and to avoid catastrophes such as this? It is incredible.
The inspection process in this country, I agree, leaves a lot to be desired, but the Government's position is that the people who entrusted their funds to, for instance, the Canadian Commercial Bank in good faith on the strength of the Government's assurances should not be penalized. What about the people who were led to believe by these Governments that everything was all right? The bail-out package which was put in place in March encourages a lot of these people to deposit their moneys in these banks. The banks themselves, in order to get these depositors, offered higher interest rates. Financial institutions actually placed funds of people in this country with these banks. How could this have been allowed to happen? What kind of conscience does this Government have to allow and to actually perpetrate this particular situation?
The Government talks about credit unions. Certainly credit unions have been hurt. People have been hurt, but how were they hurt? It was because of the fact that the Government from March of 1985, and I think before, led them down the garden path.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: That is right.

The Minister says that these people, the international banks, the banking communities, everybody has to be reimbursed, not only the small unsecured creditor, or the individual who did not have the wealth of information that the Government and the international and Canadian banks had. No, everybody has to be secured. The question is, why? Why have we got to go with this complete compensation? Why? When the Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDougall) is asked that question, she does not have an answer. Is there an international agreement that the Government has with the United States and other countries that requires investors in banks failing in any country to be completely compensated? Is
October 22, 1985

that the case? If so, the Minister should come clean to the people of Canada and to this House and state that such an arrangement is in place.
For instance, the Canadian Commercial Bank increased its share of the Westland Bank in California from 39 per cent to 100 per cent in March of 1984 in response to a cease and desist order issued against the Westland Bank by the U.S. regulator. If this bank was in difficulty in March of 1985, then it certainly was in some difficulty in March of 1984. Yet it was allowed to further invest in the Westland Bank in California.
The Hon. Member for Saskatoon East has said that it is because of the National Energy Program. People put money into the National Energy Program; this bank put money into the National Energy Program and because of the National Energy Program the economy in western Canada went downhill, and that is the reason these banks failed. The Hon. Member for Saskatoon East only has to listen to the witnesses at the Estey Commission who said that the reason these banks failed is bad loans and bad management. That is the reason these two banks failed and that is the reason this Government should have been able to spot what was happening to these banks and act in the interests of the people of this country. It should not have allowed these banks to offer higher interest rates and allowed people to invest when it knew what was going to happen. For instance, the Northland Bank on September 1 froze interest rates so people who came in after March did not get any increase in their interest rates-did not get any interest whatsoever after September 1. This is what the Government is saying they are doing to protect the people of this country.
If the Minister of State for Finance and the Government are so interested in protecting the people of the country, doing something for the people of this country with respect to banking, why are they not looking into why the banks are not offering any small business loans to regions of this country who suffer from economic disparity? Why is the Government not looking into the question of why all this money, which is being secured and guaranteed 90 per cent by the Government, is only being offered to regions of this country where the economy is successful? Why is the Government not looking into why banks are not reporting cases of computer fraud and computer crime, the cost of which is in all probability being passed back to the depositors and the people who are dealing with these banks?
It is ludicrous to say that this Government by doing this is acting on behalf of the people of this country. We heard in the May 23 Budget that the reason we were going to have to take all this hard medicine was that we had to do something about the deficit. Any reduction in the deficit has been completely neutralized by the action of this Government since then. What the people of this country have had to forfeit because of the May 23 Budget has not gone back to the individuals. It has gone to the business community in this country.
The Hon. Member for Saskatoon East said that during the National Energy Program people's businesses failed and people lost their houses. During that period of the recession

people's businesses failed and people lost their homes. I can tell the Hon. Member for Saskatoon East and members of the Government that there are still areas in the country where people are losing their homes and where businesses are failing. It is because of the fact that this Government is not looking after these people that this is still happening. It is looking after the people in the large corporations who can help themselves. In the meantime, those who need help are not receiving the attention and the legislation needed to bring them into a position in which what they are going through at the present time can be avoided.
I think what the Government is doing here is wrong. I would ask it to take note of the amendment put forward by the Right Hon. Member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Turner).

Mr. Speaker, I would like to respond to a few of the remarks made by the Hon. Member for Saskatoon East (Mr. Ravis). He referred to the time when the Liberal Government of the day expanded the banking system and, according to him-and I think rightly so-it did not make the appropriate changes in the total banking system to accommodate the expansion. It did not change the rules with respect to monitoring, inspection and so on.
There are two matters which I wish to recall in this regard. One, of course, is that I am sure the Liberals went ahead with that expansion with the support of the Conservative Party at the time, as was often the case when the Liberals changed the banking system. Second, I think it is also true that when interest rates were allowed to float in 1966, according to the theory that competition would provide interest rates at an even lower rate than 6 per cent, it was done with Conservative support over NDP opposition.
It has often been said by the Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDougall)-and I am glad she is in the House-that it was the fault of the Liberals because they did not clean up the inspection service while they had the opportunity. That is true, except for is one thing which has been left out of the Tory explanation, that is to say that in 1979 the Tory Government of the day brought in a draft Bank Act. It never had the opportunity to pass the legislation because the Government fell. However, it had an opportunity to indicate what its intentions would be with respect to the banking system.
The fact of the matter is that the Tory Bank Act of 1979, which did not receive the approval of the House, and the Liberal Bank Act of 1980, which was eventually approved by the House, are not substantially different with respect to those issues and laws which pertain to the case which we have before us. I speak of the failure of these two banks. I think it is a case of political and intellectual dishonesty for the Minister, or anyone else on the other side, to suggest that the Liberals were fundamentally different from the Conservatives in this respect because they had their chance in 1979 to indicate what they would like to do with the banking system. What they indicated

October 22, 1985
Depositors Compensation
was that they were not substantially different from the Liberals in that respect.
The Hon. Member for Saskatoon East also spoke about changing the rules. This, of course, has been a familiar Conservative complaint regarding the Liberals' management of the economy, that is, that the rules ought not to be changed. One sometimes receives the impression that the rules should never be changed, that whatever happens to be the case ought always to be the case no matter what. In any event, it is interesting that the Hon. Member for Saskatoon East made this observation because what could be a more significant changing of the rules in our economy than to depart from the principle, which has been established for some time that people with deposits of over $60,000 who are prepared to take those types of risks are, in fact, taking a risk and cannot rely upon the Government to bail them out? What the Government is doing now is fundamentally changing the rules of the banking system and, in doing so, changing people's expectations with respect to an activity that is a favourite focus of the Conservative Party. I am talking here about risk.
How many times have I sat in the House and listened to speech after speech by Conservative Members of Parliament talking about the almost mystical quality of risk-taking? They often say that risk-taking is what makes the economy go round, it is what this country was built upon. We have been told that risk-taking is this and it is that. This is the type of garbage I have had to listen to for years and years. We are now forced to suffer the indignity of seeing the Conservative Party-not the Liberals or the NDP, those anti-free enterprisers, but the Conservative Party-bail out everyone who had more than $60,000 deposited in the Canadian Commercial Bank. Anyone who deals in that amount of bread should know full well that he is taking a risk when he invests it in those banks. I find this to be an incredible irony.
The other thing I would like to say with respect to Conservative rhetoric about the bail-out has to do with the National Energy Program.
You supported it.

The Hon. Member across the way says that we supported the National Energy Program. Actually, if one were to check the record one would see that we voted against the National Energy Program. However, that type of fact does not bother the Conservatives. They have been going around the country for the last four year saying that the NDP supported the National Energy Program when, in fact, we did not. However, the facts do not seem to bother them because they are more wound up in their own mythology than what is really going on in the country. In this case they have been a victim of their own propaganda. For so long they have said that everything that is wrong with the economy in western Canada can be blamed on the National Energy Program. That has blinded them. It has made them unable to see that the problems of the Canadian Commercial Bank were not related to the National Energy Program but may well have been related-in fact, it seems to be obviously the case-to bad management and
incompetent judgment with respect to loans. Perhaps it was because the Conservative Government was fresh in office that it had not learned that the world was not the way it thought it was when it sat in opposition-1 do not know. However, being victim of its own propaganda and because it has said it so often it cannot believe otherwise. It cannot believe that problems in western Canada might be related to something other than the conspiracy against western Canada which has been going on for years, according to the Conservative Party.
I would like to say a word about that because western Canada is a much more complicated reality politically, socially and economically than what Members on the other side would like us to believe. Western Canada is not the boardrooms in Calgary. Western Canada cannot be easily and uncritically acquainted with the energy sector. Western Canada is a diversified economy. Western Canada is potash, grain, forestry, mining, manufacturing, workers and ordinary people. Western Canada is not just people who sit around worrying about what they will do with more than $60,000. I am sick and tired of having the part of the country from which I come equated with a small financial elite who sit in the boardrooms of Calgary and Edmonton. That is not what western Canada is for me. It is a much more complicated reality, which is why I can rise in my place as a western Canadian and say that no one should fall for this business. We cannot simply let the Conservatives do what they like as long as they label it as being for western Canada. They seem to think that, as long as they say that it is for western Canada, we should be quiet. Whose western Canada is it? It is not my western Canada when the Conservatives use those words.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to make some remarks on the parliamentary process which is involved in Bill C-79. First, I would like to direct some remarks to the provisions of the Bill itself.
The short title of Bill C-79 is the Financial Institutions Depositors Compensation Act. However, if one really wished to inform the Canadian public one would entitle the Bill: a Bill to restore and continue confidence in the Canadian banking system. That is what the Bill is all about. It is not directed at persons who deposited funds in the banks involved, the Northland Bank or the Canadian Commercial Bank. The real purpose of the Bill is to assure Canadians that financial investors across North America and throughout the world have confidence in the Canadian banking system and that each and every depositor, Canadian or otherwise, knows that when he puts a dollar in a Canadian bank, that dollar is protected.
I would like to ask my friends opposite, the Hon. Members of the New Democratic Party and the Liberal Party, if they would want it any other way. Would they want people to be uncertain about Canadian banking? Would they want Canadians to line up Monday morning to extract their money from our Canadian banks and destroy the economy of this country because they do not have confidence in our system? I think it has been admitted time and time again that there are remidies
October 22, 1985

which might be introduced into the system to protect us from difficulties like this in the future. I believe parliamentarians on all sides would do well to direct their minds to those solutions. But simply to cry over what has happened in the past is to be totally unconstructive both for Canada and for those people in Canada who want to invest in financial institutions.
I would direct the attention of Hon. Members opposite to the real purpose of this legislation. When those Hon. Members stand up in the House of Commons and say that this Bill ought not to be passed, that it ought to be shunted aside on the basis of the amendment which has been proposed, what they are saying to Canadians is, "We will not help you have confidence in our banking system. If you want to put a dollar into a Canadian bank, you take your chances". I do not see how that can be in the interests of Canada or in the interests of Canadian economic development. I do not know who in Canada would consider that to be a proper attitude to take. If we destroy the foundations of our economy, how can we expect our economy to grow and prosper? How can we expect Canadians to benefit?
I would like Hon. Members of the Liberal Party and the New Democratic Party to tell us what would happen in Canada if there was no confidence in our banking system.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: We have been saying it for a long time-open Government. Give us the names of those depositors, your friends.
What brought on that outburst?

Another point with respect to this Bill is the parliamentary process which is involved. I suppose, having been in opposition at one point, I would admit that there are circumstances in which prolonged debate of a Bill which is before the House of Commons is justified. I think one circumstance is when the public is not aware of the provisions of the Bill and by prolonging debate, a public information channel is created through which people can become informed. But is there anyone in Canada who does not know about the difficulties of the Northland Bank and the Canadian Commercial Bank? If there are any, I would be very much surprised. Everyone knows what happened.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: That's why we have a judicial inquiry.

Everyone knows about the decision of the Government of Canada to protect the Canadian banking system and to restore confidence in it by dealing with the problems of depositors. That is what the Bill is all about. It is that simple.
With respect to the failure of the Bill to require the depositors to be named or identified, there is a simple answer. The matter is before a commissioner, a person appointed under the Public Inquiries Act, who has all the powers and authority of a judge of the Superior Court. He has the power to summons witnesses and to look at records. That person has already been mentioned today. He is an eminent jurist and a Canadian and

I am sure Mr. Justice Estey will make the right decision in the interests of all Canadians.
If one wants to talk about governmental policy in this regard, I have in front of me an extract from the Daily News of Halifax dated October 22, 1985. It talks about the venture capital program in the great Province of Manitoba, which, as we all know, has a New Democratic Government. The headline reads, "Millionaires' interest-free loans". The millionaires in question are receiving interest-free loans from an agency of the Government of the Province of Manitoba. But what is interesting, Mr. Speaker, is that the Business Development Minister, Jerry Storie, has declined to name the firms which actually get the money when the venture capital companies use the funds. I am sure Hon. Members opposite are asking themselves, why is the Business Development Minister of the Province of Manitoba declining to name the firms which will receive the venture capital funds? That is explained by the Minister's assistant who says, and I quote:
Some investors may not want to be lined with a specific investment. The company for its own reasons may prefer not to be identified publicly.
So when members of the New Democratic Party in the House of Commons speak on the matter of identifying people who are benefiting from Government financial programs, they speak with forked tongues. They have one rule for the Government of Manitoba and another rule for the Government of Canada. But in this case, I have to agree with the Government of Manitoba-perhaps for the last time-because what is important, just as with the banking system itself, is confidence. People will not invest in banks unless they have confidence in the banking system which governs over the banks. People will not invest in enterprises, particularly venture capital enterprises in the Province of Manitoba, unless they have the confidence that the Government of Manitoba will protect the business relations which have developed with the agency of the Government of Manitoba.
I do not need to speak about the members of the Liberal Party because when they were in government their Ministers rose time after time in this House and said that the system of business relations between the Government of Canada and persons who invest in Canada, persons who are interested in building the economy of Canada, depends upon a confidential relationship. I ask Hon. Members from Newfoundland and Nova Scotia to tell me how many times they have heard that phrase in this House. How many times have they heard the Ministers in the Liberal Government stand up and say, "We must have confidence; we cannot open the files of the Government which relate to business transactions and tell everyone what the arrangement was, what the terms and conditions were"? The Liberal Party has defended that position over and over again. And we have the New Democratic Party following exactly the same policy in Manitoba. The only difference is that members of the New Democratic Party in this House of Commons can stand and irresponsibly condemn such a policy because those Hon. Members have never formed the Government of Canada and, of course, we all know they never will. We are talking about nothing in relation to this Bill.

We are talking about smoke. Every Hon. Member of the House of Commons, past, present and future, knows that there has to be confidentiality in some relationships. The Government of Canada has gone further than some people would want to go by leaving it to the Commissioner, the eminent jurist of the Supreme Court of Canada, to render a decision on the point. What more could one ask, Mr. Speaker? I think all we can ask, as supporters of the Government of Canada, is for a fair judgment by the people of Canada.
There has been an honest effort on the part of the Government, through the medium of Bill C-79, to restore the confidence of Canadians and all other investors in the Canadian banking system. That is what this Bill is, pure and simple. There has been an attempt by the Government of Canada to protect the confidential relationship which all Governments should have with people who involve themselves in transactions with Government or government agencies. Those are the two principles upon which this Bill is based. I would defy members of the Opposition to argue seriously with the merits of those two propositions: confidence in the bankins system and the confidence of the people in dealing with the Government of Canada.

I have listened with considerable interest to the Hon. Member for Halifax West (Mr. Crosby) who, on numerous occasions, has spoken out on issues which are of concern to him and to his region. He has also spoken out on some of those issues which transcend, if you will, regional concern. He uses the phrase, "Everyone knows about the Northland Bank". He uses the term "everyone". But not every Canadian knows who the uninsured depositors of that particular bank are. That is the purpose of this debate and of the amendment which has been put forward by my Leader.
It seems peculiar that members of the Government, who were adamant while in opposition about having access to information, now want to hide pertinent information from the Canadian people. You could argue with great justification that there is a cover-up. Why are they so afraid of producing the names of individuals and corporations who are going to be the recipients of millions of taxpayers' dollars? Why the cover-up? Are there certain individuals associated with those two banks who have strong Tory connections? Is that what it is? Is it because the Progressive Conservative Party of Canada has a particular sum of money deposited in one of those banks? Is that why? Or is there some other reason for which they do not wish to disclose the names? The fact of the matter is that this Government is stonewalling the Canadian people and Parliament on releasing the information we seek. That is why I ask that Members from all political Parties vote unanimously for the amendment put forward by the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner).
The Government has refused to answer the following questions, both in this Chamber and in the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs. Why did the bail-out
group not consult the CCB's external auditors? Why did the bail-out group not look at the minutes of the CCB's audit committee? Why did the Government turn down the bank's offer of a full audit of the CCB's books? We know the answer to that question despite the reluctance of the Government Members and the Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDou-gall) to provide the answer. We have concluded that a political decision was made by the Right Hon. Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mulroney), and he did so without meaningful consultation with the players involved. It was done at the beginning of a weekend during which the National Economic Conference took place here in Ottawa.
This whole deal stinks. It is absolutely worse than the tuna affair. Millions of taxpayers' dollars are being requested of the Parliament of Canada in order to bail out individuals and corporations, whether domestic or foreign, and we do not know who they are. The Minister of State for Finance has the audacity to stand in this Chamber and say to Members of Parliament and the Canadian people that there "may be" a legal opinion which says that she ought not to release the names. Therefore, the Government is in breach of one of the most fundamental rights of Parliament, the right to know. We have a right to know the names of those individuals and corporations who are going to receive large sums of taxpayers' money.
I will go one step further and charge the Minister of State for Finance with a cover-up in its worst possible form. The Government is breaching the traditions of Parliament and nullifying Parliament's duty to scrutinize every Government expenditure. However, what do we hear day in and day out from the back-benchers opposite? Somehow this is supposed to be a good move for the Canadian people. Why do Members opposite persist in allowing this cover-up to continue? The only conclusion I can reach is that they may have more information than they are giving the House of Commons and the Canadian people.
As well, Mr. Speaker, it is not fair for Members opposite to suggest that Members on this side are in any way against western institutions. That is simply not the case. The simple fact of the matter is that more than $870 million of taxpayers' money is being provided to pay for the utter incompetence of the Minister of State for Finance and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson). I could not support in good conscience the Government on this issue because there are other areas of this country in great need of financial assistance. Whether it be farmers, fishermen or people in the forest industry in British Columbia, or the people of Atlantic Canada, whom this Government has written off completely, the money should be spent there. What about daycare facilities? What about providing assistance to the thousands of municipalities across this country who have come to the Government on bended knee seeking financial assistance for such necessities as water and sewers? Those problems deserve a higher priority than the ego of the Prime Minister of this country.
It is for those reasons that I urge all Members in this Chamber, regardless of political affiliation, to examine the
October 22, 1985

amendment put forward by the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) and then vote in favour of it. If not, they will be breaching the traditions of this and of previous Parliaments of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, this Bill now before the House provides Government money to those people whose deposits in these banks in excess of $60,000 were not insured. That is the purpose of the Bill. The hon. gentleman says: "We know that". I want to drive that point home because it means that the Government of Canada is guaranteeing something which was not guaranteed before. That is the point. Well, right is right and wrong is no man's right. The reason I say that is that the Government has programs whereby it guarantees money loaned through the banks. However, when this Government took over we saw those guarantees lifted in the case of some of our primary producers. Where is the rationale for that? The poor fishermen in eastern and western Canada have this year received letters from the banks saying that the federal Government no longer guarantees their loans and therefore the banks are going to take these people to court and seize their possessions. That sounds absolutely atrocious, doesn't it? Let me read for you a letter from a bank manager to a poor Canadian fisherman concerning a loan guaranteed by the federal Government. What does the bank say? It says:
Dear Mr. Elliott,
We advise that the Federal Government is paying no further claims against Fishery Improvement loans advanced between 1977 and 1980. In this regard, we regret to inform you that your loans are now excluded from the Federal Government Guarantee, and as such, the accounts now revert to your sole responsibility.
The bank then lists the outstanding amounts. I have another letter here from a gentleman who says:
Today the sheriff brought a paper from a law firm, from St. Johns. They are going to take legal action. So what will I do?
He says:
Now, a few days ago, the bank manager phoned me. It was concerning this loan. He said if I didn't pay, that they will put the "for sale" sign on my house.
I have another letter which says:
Several years ago one couldn't walk in a bank, at least in this area, without noticing big signs saying something like, "See us for Fisheries Improvement Loans Guaranteed by the Federal Government", etc. So I, like a good many others, fell for it.
I am glad that the Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDougall) is back in the Chamber. Federal Government guarantees on loans to individuals, poor men and poor women, were lifted this year. Why? I have an official response from the Minister concerned to a constituent in Nova Scotia. He says:
While I recognize the financial difficulties you are currently experiencing, you must understand our role with the Fisheries Improvement Loans Program is that of a guarantor in the event of default by borrowers on loans registered under the
Act.
The Bank of Nova Scotia, as a result of its heavy losses, has reached its full entitlement for reimbursement by the federal Government on fisheries improve-

ment loans for the period in which your loan was registered, and therefore we can no longer be responsible for your debt.
The federal Government of this country is turning around and getting out of federal Government guarantees that were given on loans to primary producers in this country. It is backing out. However, the Bill before the Chamber is for the Government to back in. In one case it backs away from the poor man, and in another case it backs in for someone who has quite a bit of money. It backs away from a poor man, and backs in for investors. It backs away from the poor man, and backs in for municipalities and everyone else.
However, Mr. Speaker, we are not even disagreeing with that. We are asking for the names, but the Government will not even do that. Over and above all of that, Mr. Speaker, there is a basic principle involved here. Some Members in this Chamber are very angry about this Bill because of what I mentioned before; that right is right and wrong is no man's right. It is not the right of the Government to bring a Bill into this Chamber which backs in on a certain guarantee while it moves away from guarantees that were given to primary producers in this country.
Primary producers in Quebec, British Columbia, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland are today receiving letters from banks and lawyers saying that they are going to put a sign on their houses because they took out a loan with the bank that was guaranteed by the federal Government but, as the bank manager says in his letter, the federal Government has now backed out of these guarantees. In the summer of 1985 the federal Government is backing out of the guarantees which it provided on the loans that were taken out. At the same time, Mr. Speaker, we in this Chamber are debating a Bill to back in on a guarantee to people who had over $60,000 in the bank.
The Minister of State for Finance, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) should think twice. If they are going to do this for a certain group of people, they should do it for our poor primary producers as well rather than letting them hang out to dry, letting them lose their property, homes, and everything else and being dragged into court because they took out a loan guaranteed by the federal Government.
The great philosophy of the Government of Canada is to try to cut down on the deficit and to say that there will be no more giveaways. Therefore, why will the Government of Canada not tell us who is getting this $875 million? At the same time, why will it not tell us why it is backing out on its guarantees of bank loans given to primary producers in this country?

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be able to follow my eloquent colleague and add some more facts to the list. I congratulate him on his excellent address because these messages are going to be carried across the country and the Canadian people will be fully informed of what the Government is up to.

in the Canadian Commercial Bank. Now that free enterprise has been let loose the Government has encouraged people to invest their money in something that has gone bad. Approximately five years ago a Liberal Government passed a Bill to increase the insurance for depositors in banks from $20,000 to $60,000. That is the law today. That is why we have this special Bill before the House. My hon. colleague who spoke before me spoke about the fisheries and about the banks putting peoples' houses up for sale at a time when we are bailing out investors to the tune of $875 million.
Yesterday I had meetings with several municipalities about small craft harbours. There is all kinds of room for investment in the tourist industry. The people who are now sitting on the Government benches promised during the last Parliament that if they were elected they would put all kinds of money into tourism, small business, and the farming community of this country. What are they doing now? They are using the money to bail out their friends. Believe it or not, Mr. Speaker, there is no money for small craft harbours in this country. The smaller communities are being left out of the picture. I see an Hon. Member from Atlantic Canada pointing to me. Maybe he knows of some money in the Budget down there; I don't know. Mr. Speaker, the structure, length, complexity and application of the Income Tax Act has virtually destroyed any faith Canadians once had in the equity and fairness of Canada's income tax system.
Wage earners resent the bonanzas and breaks created for and used by large corporations. Farmers and small-business people seethe with frustration at the incentives and giveaways that seem only to go to enterprises large and wealthy enough to hire specialist advisers.
Bright accountants, who could be best employed advising clients on the improvement of their operations and finances, are instead applying their talents to the exploitation of socially
October 22, 1985

counterproductive loopholes which generate substantial tax savings and, therefore, larger fees.
I call upon the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Mackay) to take his sword to this Gordian knot. All the public relations, training, and procedural improvements introduced by his predecessor, worthy though they are, are only nibbling at the edges of this problem.

Mr. Speaker, it is indeed an abomination and a true miscarriage of justice to allow Dr. Mortgentaler and his associates to continue their murder of
unborn human beings at their human slaughter house at 85 Harbord Street in Toronto.
The activities of this group have consistently violated Canada's Criminal Code, by performing abortions on demand.
The Attorney General of Ontario has been derelict in his duties by refusing to exercise the powers of his office, not setting bail conditions on the accused and restraining them from further breaking of the law as they are charged pending the result of the Crown appeal of their acquittal on a similar charge.
This can be construed as the Attorney General of Ontario having no objections to Dr. Mortgentaler continuing his daily slaughter of innocent unborn human beings who cannot defend themselves or speak out on their own behalf. Each day of delay in settling this whole question means that more and more unborn babies will have their lives snatched from them. This must stop.
The most positive way in which this whole problem can be rectified is to introduce an amendment to the Charter of Rights and Freedoms that will in fact recognize, once and for all, that unborn babies are indeed persons, indeed human beings in every sense of the meaning of those words, and have the same rights, privileges, and protection under the Charter as other human beings. This action is long overdue and I therefore call upon the Government to initiate positive action in this regard as soon as possible.
