Mr. Speaker, the majority of South Africans are engaged in a struggle against racism in which increasing numbers, including children, are sacrificing their lives to prevent the murder of their souls.
They seek the achievement in their own land of a democracy based on the ideals founded on the Magna Carta, the Declaration of the Rights of Man and Citizens, and the American Declaration of Independence. They seek help from those who claim to be the defenders of those ideals of freedom and equality.
Now the Commonwealth has responded to their pleas. How much did they get? "A tiny little bit, a tiny little bit". Such is the measure of Great Britain's, and now the Commonwealth's, commitment to justice.
"It does not amount to a great deal", we are told with a pride that must not be shared by this country or its Government. We must do more than participate in merely symbolic measures or in another contact group destined to increase even more the level of frustration and resentment felt toward the western democracies.
Without the support of increased mandatory sanctions, the lip service of the West may well be replaced by the weapons of the East and the future hostility of black Africa toward the West would then be assured.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to discuss a crucial issue which affects all Canadians.

On September 26, the Prime Minister announced that Canada would be interested in seeing a new trade agreement between Canada and the United States.

Many Canadians are wary of changing the status quo, but 1 would like to assure them, and the residents of my home Province of Alberta, that a new trade agreement will improve the economic well-being of all Canadians.
In Alberta, the provincial trade situation with the United States is suffering from instability. Countervailing duties on red meats and petrochemicals are threatened against our products. More than 75 per cent of Albert's petrochemicals are sold abroad, and both the United States and Canada impose tariffs ranging from 10 per cent to 18 per cent.
Alberta exports in 1984 totalled $10.6 billion, which equalled $4,500 per capita. Of this total, $9.3 billion went to the United States, which equalled $4,000 per capita.
1 conducted a survey last spring in my own riding of Edmonton South and found that 65 per cent were in favour of freeing up our trade arrangements with our neighbour to the south.
I applaud the Government's initiative. Not to conduct these negotiations would be to shy away from our responsibility to enhance the prosperity of our nation. 1 can assure not only Albertans but all Canadians that a new trade agreement with the United States will benefit us all.

ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY WELLAND CANAL BLOCKAGE-EFFECT ON GRAIN EXPORTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Government's cut-backs in funding to the St. Lawrence Seaway in last May's Budget threaten this vital transportation link be-
October 22, 1985

tween western Canada and the eastern seaboard. Prairie grain producers depend on access to world markets through the St. Lawrence Seaway system.
The recent wall collapse in the Welland Canal, the second major disruption of the Seaway in a year, demonstrates the need to maintain the Seaway properly. This week over 70 ships are trapped in the system. The Government must move quickly to see that the disruption does not affect the delivery of millions of tonnes of grain on its way to customers abroad. The Government must take action to assure our grain customers abroad that Canada continues to be a secure supplier of grain to the world market-place.
The current Welland Canal blockage places hundreds of farmers in financial jeopardy at a time when farm incomes are at a record low. In the May, 1985 Budget, the Government announced that it was taking $30 million away from the St. Lawrence Seaway Authority. This action demonstrates the Government's irresponsible attitude toward this vital transportation link.
I call upon the Government to reverse this decision and to take every action necessary to get these grain shipments moving to the world market.

Mr. Speaker, all of Canada commends the excellent energy agreements the Government has concluded-the Western Accord and the Atlantic Accord. There is increased activity on provincial lands in the fields of exploration, development and production, and this means jobs, jobs, jobs.
On behalf of the industry I should like to urge the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Miss Carney) to give priority to the following areas of concern. First is the elimination of the 25 per cent back-in and all associated provisions. This has amounted to confiscation, and results in disincentives. The Canadian ownership rate, or the COR content, should apply only at the development stage, not at the exploration stage.
Royalties should be lowered or forgone on Canada Lands until pay-out is reached. Due to the extremely high cost of exploration and development, this would result in accelerated growth. maintopic: NON-SMOKING CAMPAIGN-STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the House for its co-operation and I will not be very long.
Earlier today the Government of Canada, along with most of the provincial and territorial Governments and, most impor-
October 22, 1985

tant, various voluntary organizations, launched a non-smoking campaign directed primarily at Canadian youth between the ages of 12 and 19. This national program to reduce smoking is a long-term and comprehensive approach to the reduction of smoking among Canadians. It focuses on both smoking prevention and cessation strategies, with special attention given to high risk groups.
I also want to say, Mr. Speaker, that there are organizations which have been in the lead in this area and have been doing an exemplary job. As I said at the press conference, possibly Government have joined them, rather than the other way around. They have been indicating that smoking and secondary smoke is a major health issue and, of course, the Government of Canada concurs with that. Organizations such as the Canadian Lung Association, the Canadian Council on Smoking and Health, the Canadian Cancer Society, the Canadian Medical Association, the Canadian Pharmaceutical Association and the Canadian Public Health Association had all joined previous to today. I am happy to report that the Canadian Heart Foundation has today agreed to join as well.
I believe this is a collective action, Mr. Speaker. We have proposed an advertising campaign which has been launched. We are using media that will appeal to young people, including rock videos and advertising, which meets head on the issue of others trying to convince young people to take up the habit.
I am sure that Members are aware that approximately
30,000	Canadian deaths per year are directly attributable to smoking and secondary smoking. I am pleased with the cooperation that has been shown by so many. The message will be called "Break Free". I believe that we have to show young people especially that a lifestyle without smoking is acceptable even to their peer groups. We all recognize that that is a major task for us all.
I want to indicate to the House that within the Department of National Health and Welfare we have established a nonsmoking policy today. There are some Departments and some government agencies which have already taken this initiative. Within the Department of National Health and Welfare we took a survey of employees asking them various questions relating to the setting up of smoke-free environment in the national capital and specifically in the Department of National Health and Welfare. The majority of employees wish to have a policy which would minimize smoke in the working environment and also accommodate employees who smoke in certain areas outside the immediate working environment. That policy will come into effect on January 1, 1986. I am also pleased to announce that there is agreement between the employees' associations and the Public Service Alliance.
I think that all Canadians recognize that the Government of Canada must be more involved in preventive measures to maintain health. In my mind, there is no single issue which is more directly attributable to a lifestyle habit such as smoking and I commend the program to the House and to Canadians in general. I am pleased that radio stations, television companies
Statements by Ministers
and some newspapers have taken initiatives by declaring some of their own offices smoke-free areas as well as by not accepting written advertising from tobacco companies. Those are steps in the right direction. I thank them for their co-operation.
Finally, I would like to thank as well Members opposite for their support of this program. We have much distance to cover, but I believe that because what we have launched today is a co-operative effort it should bear results. I thank the House for its time.

Mr. Speaker, I always appreciate your recognition on matters of such importance to the Canadian public. During this debate a number of Members from this side of the House have stated their serious reservations about the Government's conduct in this matter which is so crucial to the Canadian public.
This debate in itself proves the value of Parliament because it is giving time for Canadians to absorb fully and understand the enormity of what has taken place as a result of the incompetent way the Government has handled this matter. There is an increasing anger on the part of Canadians about what has transprired.
During the four or five days I spent in western Canada I was interested to listen to the comments about the so-called bank crisis. There is a growing wave of anger about the way this situation was handled. People do not like to see a Government expediently and conveniently deal with a matter so fundamental to their livelihood on the basis of what were obviously political considerations.
As we know, the banking system has been the central framework in this country for a long time. This is particularly true in the last 10 years, since the amendments to the Bank Act were introduced by previous Liberal Governments. This attempt to give opportunities for smaller banks to emerge and provide a different regime of loans for small businesses in regions of the country was particularly appreciated.
The progress we made in developing that new facet or thrust of the banking system has now been lost. Perhaps it has been irrevocably lost, but it has certainly been lost for a good deal of time. There is a loss of confidence, faith and trust. That loss is mirrored in the same emotions which people now have for the Government of Canada, that loss of confidence, faith and trust. For all the other fumbles, bumbles and stumbles committed by the Government during the last several months, the one which goes to the heart of the matter is its handling of the banking situation.
People are angry about it because they suspect that it is a cover-up. They suspect that too much is being hidden. They suspect that too many people may be benefiting for actions which, in themselves, were foolhardy and reckless to begin with. They wonder why the Government is asking for hundreds of millions of dollars of taxpayers' money and is reluctant to come clean on who is to benefit. They wonder why there is such a concerted effort to skirt the issue.
Even with the proclamation of the commission under Mr. Justice Estey, it is clear that many areas of vital public concern relating to the handling of the banking crisis will not be covered by that commission. It goes back to what we saw exemplified time and time again in the handling and management of the Government. Perhaps it is what one would call the mushroom theory of Government-throw unto them those products which are most energetically manufactured by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), keep them in the dark and they will grow. People are becoming a little tired of that. Anger is beginning to devleop. They feel that there was a system of protection for those who legitimately had insured investments.
Why is it that suddenly hundreds of millions of dollars are being provided to categories, not to individuals, corporations or entities? We do not know who is responsible or who in fact will
October 22, 1985

be paid off. I think the Government owes it to Canadians to answer that question. It is essential, if the Government is to come before Parliament asking for extravagant sums of money. We are not talking about trifling sums; we are talking about hundreds of millions of dollars. Surely that, by every canon of parliamentary responsibility, requires a Government to explain itself and to be forthright. It should come before Parliament and explain exactly who is on the receiving end. That is not taking place.
I read with interest a letter which was received in my office just today. It is from a gentleman who lives in my constituency. In fact, he is a former member of the Legislative Assembly of Manitoba with a very distinguished career. It reads:
I am a director in a small oil company; as you can see by the enclosed copy of our last nine months financial statement we put $6,000 into the Canadian Commercial Bank. You will note the much higher interest rate they were offering than the other banks.
As an aside, I should like to indicate that at the same time Scotiabank was offering 8.25 per cent, Canadian Commercial Bank was offering 10.25 per cent. Its rate was 3 points higher in the same period of time. The letter continues:
I feel people who go for the highest interest should be prepared to place their capital at risk and, if through greed and poor judgment lose, then so be it.
By passing the bail-out Bill before the House now, it will only encourage investors to always go for the highest interest rate because the federal Government by this precedent will always bail them out! Don't let them pass it and let the bells ring till an election is called.
That is the voice of one person, a person who has some experience both in business and in Government. He is saying that the Bill has an implication which goes far beyond-and I know that that in itself sounds extravagant-just the hundreds of millions of dollars which will be taken out of the Canadian economy and passed back into the hands of unknown holders. There will also be a precedent set. How can the Government, from this point onward, deny other financial institutions? Does it not begin to give licence to those institutions to say that they can go for the high roll? Could they not play ricochet with Canadian money? If they are lucky and get a good take, they will be very prosperous. However, if they fail, they can always go to the Government to be bailed out because the Government bailed the others out. Why would it be any different? A precedent is being set.
I find it discouraging to look at the statements made by the Minister who presented the Bill and the supporting words of her colleagues on the other side of the House. They do not seem to seize fully the severity and seriousness of what they are doing. They are really setting in motion what lawyers would call a stare decisis which will haunt successive Governments for years to come.
The only way in which the Government could possibly eliminate that founding precedent is to provide us with a clear justification as to why this is such an exceptional case and why this should be given an exceptional judgment. Yet the Government has not been prepared to do that. It has not given the kind of information which Parliament requires in order to make a judgment. We oppose this amendment with sorrow but we also share in the anger of many other Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, the Bill before us is one of utmost urgency. The Hon. Member for Renfrew-Nipissing-Pembroke (Mr. Hopkins) spoke about the urgency of moving to some matter about which he was concerned. However, 1 must say how urgent I feel it is to move to the disposition of this Bill. I do not want to prolong the debate, therefore my remarks will be brief. However, I should like to direct them specifically to what the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy) said. He talked about the unfortunate precedent which the Bill may presage. His comments will end up being irrelevant because we will have a totally different regulatory framework for the future. Precedents of a past period will not be relevant into the future because there will be a new regulatory framework. That is what the Minister and the Standing Committee have been working hard to put in place. A new framework, new rules, a strengthened Inspector General of Banks and a strengthened set of regulations will totally exclude any possibility of these kinds of precedents being directly relevant.
Secondly, the previous speaker mentioned the mushroom theory of Government. This Bill really addresses the mushroom theory of banks. What happened was that in 1980, suddenly mushrooming into the Canadian economy, instead of a handful of banks were 70 banks. They were put in a framework that lacked, in my view, the regulatory parameters and the strength in the Inspector General's office to allow these banks to operate with confidence and with effectiveness. It is the mushroom theory of banks with improper regulation that has got us into trouble, not the mushroom theory of Government.

He speaks of loss of confidence and the loss of trust in the Government because of this particular Bill. If western banks are viewed as not being as important as central Canadian banks that would lead to loss of trust and loss of confidence in this country in terms of unfairness.
My riding in London, Ontario is the home of many trust companies and insurance companies. One would think that my constituents would not be interested in the viability of western banks. They are. They believe that, for a united country which is fair to all regions, western banks are important to the fabric of the western economy just as, for example, financial institutions like Canada Trust are vital to the economy of southwestern Ontario. The Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry also discussed how delicate and how important the banking system is. That is precisely what we are addressing and what we have been addressing for the last few months with the Green Paper on financial institutions, with this legislation and with many other initiatives that this Government has taken in order to strengthen the confidence that people can have in our banking system.
This leads me to my final comment which is that if we follow the advice of the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry, and his leader, and reveal the names of all the depositors, what would that do to our banking system internationally? What would that to do our banking system and the confidence that people would feel in it? Confidentiality is the bedrock of the Bank Act and if we are going to change that we do not change it in the middle of some sort of episode like this. I may remind Hon. Members here in the House that $60,000 is quite a lot of money. In fact, the vast majority of Canadians cannot hope to save that much in their entire lifetime. Sixty thousand dollars is a lot of money for most Canadians.
And now, not only does the Government want to compensate these people, something I entirely agree with, but it has introduced Bill C-79 in order to compensate all those depositors with accounts considerably in excess of $60,000. In many cases, we are talking about depositors with accounts worth several hundred thousand dollars. And the Government is saying that we need this legislation to cover these fantastic sums of money in order to maintain confidence in the Canadian banking system!

They decided to leave their money on deposit so the system would get back on an even keel, hoping things would turn out all right. These are the kind of people who can be found in my constituency of Verdun-Saint-Paul, people who have invested some of their savings in pension plans, workers and ordinary Canadians who had and still have confidence in the Government. The question is quite simple: Can we really afford to tell those people: "They made a mistake, and because of this you lose all your money; just stay home, there is nothing left for you''. Or should we tell them: "You tried to help, you really tried to stabilize those two banks. But there we are. I notice that the Opposition today is constantly criticizing, implying that those people with more than $60,000 are really anonymous people, rich people from abroad, or rich people always trying to put their money in biding. But it may be about time that we tell Canadians, Quebecers, many of whom are wondering: Who are those people actually? Who are those people who invested over $60,000? Well, they are municipalities that need the money to better stabilize their affairs, to do better work, to better invest in their communities.
Look at the City of Verdun again, for instance. Our community is currently going through difficult times. The economy is at a very low ebb, and working capital is hard to get. Are we

Second, this energy path is a path with profound implications and one which has been imposed upon Canadians in an undemocratic way by a technocratic elite without adequate public discussion and with the acquiescence of politicians who have been held captive by the mystique and indeed the tyranny of expertise and the so-called value-free advice they receive from such experts.
One of the few value-free facts that attends a debate on the nuclear issue is the fact that most of the so-called facts are laden with assumptions.What is needed is a real debate about those assumptions and values and not the usual frustrating debate that often occurs with AECL or Ontario Hydro types on the one hand who pretend or worse, actually believe that they are objective while patronizing their opponents as being those who bring only emotional arguments to the table and on the other hand anti-nuclear energy representatives who are trying to move the debate to a more fundamental level. As moral agents, we are all equally able to imagine and choose between human futures. At that level, there is no hiding behind a degree in physics or engineering. Today I want to do a little of that kind of reflection, keeping in mind that we are talking about conflicting world views or paradigms and not a phoney conflict between facts and values.
Let us begin with uranium mining, a sore spot for many Members of the New Democratic Party as it is the one link in the nuclear fuel cycle in which the Party has acted out of line with the view that I am putting forward today. Uranium mining in Canada ought to be stopped for a number of reasons. It is unacceptable because it involves Canada in the nuclear arms race. It is destructive and dangerous to the long-term health of the environment. It often happens in areas that are the traditional homelands of native peoples and the mining is done in such a way as to destroy the viability of the renewable resource economy on which they depend for an economically reliable and healthy lifestyle.
The persistent and not unfounded belief that Canadian uranium is making its way into nuclear bombs and/or freeing up other uranium for nuclear bombs should be cause for national shame. It gives the lie to all the ways in which we Canadians like to think that our hands are clean when it comes to the nuclear arms race. Our hands are not clean; they are dirty. Every time any provincial or federal Government promotes uranium mining as an economic benefit they are guilty of falling into the sin warned against by the biblical warning: What shall it profit a man if he should gain the whole world, but lose his soul? In trying to build economic prosperity on activities such as uranium exports, knowing full well that we
October 22, 1985

are contributing to the proliferation of nuclear weapons, we as a country are selling our souls in a bargain which requires of us increasing measures of oppression, lies and ecological irresponsibility. The alternative vision is to see that an economy based on such moral bankruptcy is no economy at all and to begin now the support of sustainable and ecologically acceptable economic strategies based on renewable resources, renewable sources of energy and fully human development as opposed to the kind of devastating short-lived and short-sighted economic development that has been so prominent in our past.
The CAN DU reactor is another aspect of the Canadian nuclear picture which deserves a great deal of attention. A question by me to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Miss Carney) last fall revealed a great deal about the Government's attitude and lack of ability to ask fundamental questions. I asked the Minister if the new Government intended to live up to the Conservative promise in 1979 to initiate a parliamentary inquiry into the whole nuclear fuel cycle. The Minister replied with no hint of embarrassment that the problem with the nuclear industry might only be a marketing one and that she would check with AECL to see if they thought an inquiry was necessary. This was my first strong hint of the purely commercial plane on which the Minister of Energy thinks. It surfaces again with respect to Canadian research into radioactive waste disposal, which I will deal with later.
For now, suffice it to say that it is not just a problem of marketing. The real question is whether we should be marketing nuclear reactors in the first place, not how we could be better at marketing them. This is something that inquiries such as I have asked for could reflect on and, while doing so, it would be nice to reflect on just how the Candu reactor has come to hold such a privileged position in the Canadian technological pantheon. It often seems to me that what has made the incredible subsidization of the nuclear industry possible is the way in which this technological vanity of ours somehow symbolizes for some Canadians our claim to fame in the modern world. This accommodation to the way of the world is something that should be questioned. I would rather our national sense of self-worth was derived from the extent to which, as a country, we were pursuing alternatives to the centralized technological industrial paradigm that is eating away at the future of our planet and the possibilities for a fully human future.
A third aspect of the nuclear fuel cycle which I would like to deal with is the question of radioactive waste disposal. This is a question which has occuppied me in general for some years now; but I have been particularly involved in it through the debate concerning the Underground Research Laboratory at Lac du Bonnet, Manitoba, near Pinawa, going back to May 1980 when I first raised the issue in the House of Commons. At that time I was asking, in co-operation with the Committee of Concerned Citizens in Manitoba, for public hearings into the underground radioactive waste disposal research project
Nuclear Power
which AECL had begun in that area. The Liberal Government of the day refused such hearings and the project went ahead. Since then, the debate about the URL has centred around the question of whether or not the site at Lac du Bonnet should or could ever be considered as a permanent site for disposal of radioactive waste. The NDP Government of Manitoba has said that in its view this is not an option. Unfortunately, no current Government can speak for all future Governments. Even more unfortunately, the current federal Minister of Energy has been unwilling to rule out Lac du Bonnet as a permanent site. Instead, she has created even more anxiety by commenting in a letter to the Town Council of Gimli, who had written her about this issue, about the possible commercial benefits to Canada if we decided to take in the radioactive garbage of the world and dispose of it deep in the Canadian Shield. I have to suppose that this would be part and parcel of the new improved marketing strategy of the Government. We will provide cradle-to-grave services for all our nuclear customers-only Canada will be the grave, the grave for tons and tons of radioactive waste produced elsewhere by our technologies. What a vision! It seems to me that it must take a particular kind of darkness of the mind to see light in such a picture of the future.
Having said that, I want it to be clear that I am not against such research. We have to dispose of what we already have in the best way possible. I am against research which is part of a general approach oriented toward the goal of making the world more likely to produce more such wastes. We should be worried enough about whether we can safely store what we have already produced without asking for more trouble. For this reason, I think that AECL should be stripped of its responsibility for waste disposal and it should be given over to the Department of the Environment and completely separated from AECL, which, in my view and in the view of many people who have paid attention to this issue, is in a conflict of interest that can no longer be tolerated.
In any event, anxiety in Manitoba has been greatly increased of late by the interest taken in the URL in Lac du Bonnet by the U.S. Department of Energy whose interest, I am sure, is more than purely academic or idle curiosity. In fact, it will be able to explore in Manitoba what it has been unable to explore without the co-operation of northern American states which share a similar geography with Manitoba. I know that there are Minnesotans who are concerned about that as well. Manitoba, with no uranium mining and no nuclear power, should be one of the last places to be considered as a site for radioactive waste disposal. Canada- whatever we finally do with our radioactive wastes-should not get into the business of promoting more waste or the importation of it.
Whether in terms of long-term damage to the environment through uranium mining, reactors, radioactive waste, low level radiation, or whatever, or in terms of the sudden and comprehensive destruction of a nuclear war followed by nuclear winter, the nuclear issue raises moral questions of the highest order-questions of inter-generational morality which have

October 22, 1985
Nuclear Power
been seldom, if ever, raised by previous technologies or available human choices. In pursuing the nuclear option, we are running a risk for the future of our planet that we have no right to take, especially here in Canada where we have the social, economic and political capacity to happily pursue other energy paths, other economic strategies that do not elevate the short-term needs of one generation at the expense of all others to come in the name of a false confidence in our ability to solve all our problems with a technological solution. This false confidence in the technological solution is nothing other than the modern equivalent of the ancient cult of Baal, whereby man sought to manipulate the gods instead of trusting in the promises of God to deliver us from the enemies of life if only we would seek first His kingdom and His justice. The nuclear option is not the only place in modern life where we opt for this kind of unfaithfulness and idolatry. However, for me, and I think for many others as well, it is the central symbol of that idolatry, whether it takes the form of nuclear energy or nuclear weapons. How long we can pursue this idolatrous course without the kind of judgment that those who worship Baal met is not for me to presume. If we do not escape the awful future we are building for ourselves and we do have a nuclear war, it will not be the happy cosmological shoot-out between good and evil which lunatics like Jerry Falwell think it will be. Instead, it will be a judgment on all those who trusted in their horses and chariots instead of justice.
It has been one of the greatest frustrations of my half dozen years here in the House of Commons that I have not been able, along with a handful of others who I know share my concern, to have the nuclear energy question placed higher on the agenda for public discussion and reflection. There has been more debate about nuclear weapons; but even that has not often been enough related to the ways in which the conflict of interest which might precipitate a nuclear war are intimately connected to the false need to protect the way of live which is so well represented by the nuclear energy option-a way of life captive to the domination and exploitation of non-renewable energy resources and a way of life that is ever more captive to corresponding images of national security and the loss of freedom that can flow from the authority of such images.
The nuclear energy option needs to be debated. Canadians are still waiting for an opportunity to say what they think and to reflect together on their common future. I hope that in providing this one small occasion for such a debate, I will have contributed in my own way to that day when we finally wake up to the hidden and, in my view, mistaken assumptions which have made the nuclear industry so sacred in this country.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened quite patiently during the speech of the Hon. Member and I believe he raised the subject of the Clark Government and that it raised this subject as a public issue. I believe 1 can discuss some of the things the Hon. Member raised and if he does not like it, that is too bad, but he should be polite enough to listen to other people.
At the same time as the Hon. Member was talking about some things in the past, I think it would be appropriate to ask him if he does not think in proposing this moratorium he is throwing out the baby with the bath water? Does the Hon. Member want to throw out some of the things our nuclear industry has brought us such as the cobalt treatment which is used for cancer radiation? Does the Hon. Member want to stop the irradiation of food which is being carried out in order to preserve life and make for healthier people in the Third World where there is no refrigeration? Does the Hon. Member want to close down the nuclear isotopes factory in Kanata which produces nuclear medicine? There are a number of things which have been promoted and have been very beneficial not only to Canadians but to other people in the world and these things have come about as a result of nuclear power.
This country has been in the forefront of nuclear technology for 40 years. Nuclear power is one of the most complex technologies of the 20th century. It presents great challenges to policy makers due to the wide ranging technical, health, environmental, political and ethical questions it raises. For that entire 40 years Canada has been pledged to the peaceful use of nuclear technology and I believe we have done a very good job, by and large, on that. I do not want to minimize the fact that there are some problems which have to be dealt with and I have some sympathy with what the Hon. Member has to say, especially in the area of waste management. I am not particularly happy with the dragging of the feet in dealing with that topic. I remember back in the 1970s we were promised that matter would be pretty well solved by the mid-1980s. Here we are in the mid-1980s and now they are talking about the year 2000.
Nuclear Power
There are points on both sides but I feel to a great extent the benefits we in Canada have received to date outweigh the negatives with which we must deal. There is the negative in the ultimate use of nuclear bombs which has fortunately not taken place to a degree which has wiped out more than two cities and quite a few hundreds of thousands of people, which happened during a state of war many years ago. Hopefully, we in this world have learned something since then.
I would like to talk about the benefits we have received following a Canadian policy of peaceful use of nuclear energy. The Candu reactor is still one of the star performers on the national and international scene. I believe the last time I looked at the figures I saw that six out of the ten most efficient nuclear reactors in the world are the Candu reactors. Candu provides significant benefits to the Canadian economy of which there are many spin-offs. I know there are over 1,000 people employed in my constituency and many more than that in the constituency to the northwest, Renfrew, Nipissing and Pembroke. In 1984, nuclear power generated 12 per cent of Canada's electricity and will contribute about 20 per cent by the early 1990s. I believe it should be pointed out that in Ontario and New Brunswick nuclear energy today provides more than a third of our electricity requirements. Obviously we cannot just close that down. If we did close it down, what are the alternatives? We have dammed virtually all the rivers we can in Ontario. We would have to go to coal which is the only other source.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   NUCLEAR POWER ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: How about becoming energy efficient?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   NUCLEAR POWER ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
I am sure the Hon. Member will have the chance of opening his mouth at an appropriate time.
Ontario will produce over 60 per cent of its electricity by cost effective nuclear power by the early 1990s. There is no reason to impose a moratorium on nuclear power. It is safe, economical and environmentally benign. The system is working. We can always work to improve it but I do not think we should discard it.
The nuclear power generated in this country has proven safe. We have over 100 reactor years of operation in Canada without a radiation-related fatality. Ontario Hydro statistics show its nuclear workers are safer on the job than when away from work. Nuclear power is economical. Ontario electricity consumers have already saved some $2 billion through using nuclear rather than the only practical alternative, coal. In addition, Canada is saved from having to import almost $1 billion of coal annually from the United States.
A lot of the experts in the field now agree that the disposal of nuclear wastes should provide no problems. In fact the problems have not been solved, obviously to the satisfaction of the Hon. Member who introduced the motion. Nor have they been solved to my satisfaction. I am most anxious for them to get going and work on that problem. I am not willing to listen only to the AECL assessment. However, I believe we have to consider that in Canada we have received an awful lot of benefit from the continuing use of nuclear power. I do not think we have any immediate alternatives. Obviously we

October 22, 1985
Nuclear Power
cannot get rid of one-third of our power supply in Ontario overnight without considering what we have to replace it with, that is coal. Coal will, on the evidence, produce acid rain which will ruin our lakes, our forests, and cause a great amount of concern for those with environmental sensitivities. We would cause more problems with coal.
Why do we need a commission of inquiry? The nuclear industry is probably the most examined industry in Canada's history. The Ontario Royal Commission on Electric Power Planning has looked into this matter exhaustively. The previous and current Ontario select committees on hydro affairs have done the same. Federal and provincial environmental assessment panels have examined proposals for uranium mining and refinery expansion activities and the Candu reactor on many occasions. Various studies have been commissioned by the federal Government, such as the Canadian Nuclear Industry's Marketing Performance, and a strategy for developing and strengthening the Canadian nuclear industry. There have been nuclear policy review background papers, the Nuclear Industry Review Problems and Prospects, 1981 to the year 2000. They go on and on. None of these inquiries or studies has recommended a moratorium on nuclear power. All have recommended continuing the use of nuclear power where it is economically advantageious to do so. It is also interesting to note that previous inquiries have generated very limited public interest. The Hon. Member indicated in his speech that only a limited handful of people in the House supported his views. I must admit that when he said that it struck me that democracy was truly speaking. He does not claim he could persuade a majority of this House or a majority of Canadians to his view.
The Porter Commission, which sat for many years, developed very little public following or interest. The Ontario select committee hearings had virtually zero public attendance. Church sponsored hearings into nuclear issues held last year in Toronto were given little attention by the public and even less by the press. The previous NDP sponsored debate in this House in February of 1984 on the subject of a nuclear inquiry played to an almost empty House, including the press and public galleries. Why, then, do we need to have another commission of inquiry? Why do we need to have a national referendum? The choice of alternative electricity generating modes is based on complex technical, financial and economic analysis and it would be highly inappropriate to have a decision such as that taken by way of a referendum. Furthermore, under our system of parliamentary democracy, I do not believe referendums should ever be used altough some consider they may be used on occasion. I happen to believe that when you are elected as a Member of Parliament, you are elected to make a decision. If you have not been making good solid decisions over your term in office then the people, in their own way, will decide they do not want your decision-making ability anymore and will throw you out at the next election.
Canada has a nuclear record of which we can be proud. Yes, there can be concerns. Yes, we can always fan embers into
flames. However, this is a case where we have to consider all the other options available. We have to consider what has really been done, and not just make inflammatory statements which can be used in a demogogic way. We also have to recognize that the process can be enhanced through the peaceful use of nuclear energy. I do not think we sat back and decided whether we wanted a commission on whether we should use wheels or not. Wheels are also used in warfare and as society moved on we tried to adapt new inventions to peaceful use, at least in the majority of cases. The Candu technology, of which we can be justifiably proud, is one which has received an awful lot of support and accolades from around the world. Candu has been judged to be the most reliable and efficient reactor in the world. The nuclear industry in this country has been supported to a great degree by Governments because of the many beneficial spin-offs which have helped manking. I am thinking of cobalt treatments and the manufacturing of those devices by AECL to be sold to about 60 countries around the world. A process for irradiating food has been developed and it is being used in Third World countries to preserve food in fit condition for human consumption much longer than would otherwise be possible. Then we have nuclear medicine and a number of other uses for nuclear isotopes which are for peaceful purposes and mankind's gain.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must say that this Bill is the most retrograde piece of legislation I have ever in this House of Commons. The Hon. Member had some very interesting things to say. He quoted from the scripture: "What shall it profit a man if he gains the whole world and loses his soul?" Let me say to him that when it comes to energy in Canada the NDP have already lost their soul. It was rather interesting when the Hon. Member for Pembina (Mr. Elzinga) put the question to him about a
October 22, 1985

national referendum. He wants a national referendum after his great research into the nuclear industry in Canada but he does not want a national referendum on capital punishment. I suppose he would not want a referendum on abortion or the rest of these moral issues, yet he is talking about nuclear energy as a moral issue. An Hon. Member says "job creation", and I am going to come to that.
The Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie) talked about the moral issue. Quite often I have heard speakers from his Party talk about how worried they are about the futur of their children and their children's children with regard to atomic energy. Let me suggest to the Member that the scientists, technicians and other people who work at Atomic Energy of Canada Limited or any other related industry also have children and their children will have children. Is he really saying, in a very moral way, to all those top scientists, researchers, labourers and technicians who work in those plants that they do not care for their children or their children's children? You bet they do.
We had up to 2,350 employees working at Atomic Energy of Canada Limited at Chalk River until the axe of the Tory Government fell. Those people are my neighbours. They live in good clean communities. They go to work every day and their health is checked out. There are professional doctors at the plant. They have a biology unit and there are people who take soil samples. I wish the Hon. Member would go into one of these industries once in a while to really find out what they are all about.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   NUCLEAR POWER ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: I have been there.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   NUCLEAR POWER ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
He talks about the emotional argument of Ontario Hydro and the nuclear industry. What could be more emotional, Mr. Speaker, than the speech he delivered today trying to put fear into the minds of people? I totally agree that the Candu reactor is the safest reactor in the world. He got that little piece in there too relating to the peaceful uses of nuclear energy; not really defining them, but relating them to the atomic bomb. That is where he went wrong. If the Hon. Member and his Party do not have the foresight to support the high technology that we have today in nuclear energy in the future, if they want to destroy that industry, they are inviting Canadians to return to the dark ages. All they need do is look at the oil industry and the gas resources of this country.
The Member is talking about alternate energy, Mr. Speaker. Alternate energy is a very, very small fraction of the energy that this country will need in the future.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   NUCLEAR POWER ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Because of people like you.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   NUCLEAR POWER ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Twenty years from now he will have to live with himself if nuclear energy for peaceful purposes is destroyed in this country because of the kind of argument that we are hearing today.
Let us talk about jobs. If Ontario Hydro had not taken part in the nuclear energy program, one-third of the industries in
Nuclear Power
the Province of Ontario would not have the energy to operate today. We would not have that "golden horseshoe" around Toronto, Oshawa, Hamilton, and Burlington. We would not have the population growth. What does the Member want to do? I always thought that New Democratic Party members were great environmentalists. Does he want to block up every river in this country? Does he want to block up James Bay and flood a large part of northern Ontario? That is one of the alternatives. Yet he says he is concerned about native property and native rights in Canada. He is not concerned about native rights if he is going to try to get enough hydro out of water resources for alternate energy to run this nation because he will not be able to find it. Canadian oil resources will be depleted and we will need something on which to run this country 10 years from now.
I very seriously suggest to the Hon. Member that his children and his children's children are going to ask their grandfather, the former Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill who is here in the House today, where he was when they needed him. We will have to spend billions of dollars importing energy. Since nuclear energy has come into the Province of Ontario it has saved the province in the neighbourhood of $4 billion on the purchase of coal from the United States. That is exported cash. Instead, we are using our own intellectual community, our own health care community, and our own labour resources to develop the Candu reactor which is the safest reactor on the face of the earth today.
The Member wants to represent labour in Canada as a New Democratic Party member. What is he going to say to labour when there is no energy to run the factories? What is he going to say to consumers in any part of Canada that operates a Candu reactor to produce hydroelectric power when their hydro bill increases by 40 per cent? The four Candu reactors at Pickering alone produce more hydroelectric power than it was ever dreamed would be produced by Niagara Falls. If we did not have those four Candu reactors every household in this country would pay 40 per cent more for their energy source.
This has other implications. If the hydro bills of consumers are going to increase 40 per cent because we have not made use of nuclear energy, what will happen to the manufacturing industry in the industrial core of Canada? Imagine how competitive we would be on the world market today if a Bill such as this, which virtually condemns nuclear energy, had been passed? We think we are having trade problems now, but they would be nothing compared to the problems we would have if we did not have cheap nuclear energy from Candu reactors.
I cannot help but feel very sad for people who condemn nuclear energy. They are really condemning the professional community of Canada which works with it. They do not tell us that the cobalt therapy unit for cancer treatment was produced by Atomic Energy of Canada Limited. They do not mention that because it is too good an argument. The Hon. Member for Lanark-Renfrew-Carleton (Mr. Dick) mentioned medical radio isotopes which have become one of our greatest exports in high technology in this field. We produce many, many of these in Canada and ship them out and it is making money.

October 22, 1985
Nuclear Power
I want to conclude by saying that the people of Canada should not take this Bill seriously. The Porter Commission met for months and conducted hearings. While many people appeared before that Commission, there were very few of the public present. Raising fears and killing the Candu reactor, which is one of the finest high-tech and scientific processes, for energy production is like killing the future of this country.
The New Democratic Party can sponsor Bills like this as long as they want but they are condemning high-tech research in this country and condemning Canadians to higher costs of living, higher heating costs and condemning the industrial community in Canada to higher production costs. They will create a total lack of employment for Canadians in many areas of this country.
I suggest that we should follow the positive thinkers in the House and proceed with Atomic Energy of Canada research. We have the professionals who are capable of looking after our health and safety as we progress in this country. Let us not relate the peaceful uses of one of the finest industries in Canada to an atomic bomb. That is a phoney issue he has raised and does not reflect the serious effects which this Bill would have on the Canadian economy as a whole.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   NUCLEAR POWER ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to take part in the debate on Bill C-231, which concerns nuclear power. The purpose of this Bill is to ask the Parliament of Canada to impose a moratorium on the use of nuclear power in order to proceed with a public inquiry on nuclear power, followed by a referendum.
Mr. Speaker, I intend my contribution to this debate to be constructive, realistic and to have a sense of perspective. It is not surprising that a Bill of this kind should be on the Table of the House today. There is ample justification for such a Bill, because we do not want to repeat past mistakes, especially if we recall that this year marks the 40th anniversary of the first time the atomic bomb was used. People are increasingly concerned about the use of nuclear power, and peace movements and environmentalists are making us listen to their concerns, which is a very good thing.
The general concept is of course a very valid one. However, it is very hard to visualize the logistics or the practical ramifications of such a project. Consulting the people is un-doutedly an excellent expression of parliamentary democracy. Given every person a chance to say what they think about a given subject would clearly show that in our political system, there is a very close relationship between the governing and the governed. However, Mr. Speaker, and I am speaking from my experience as mayor and as president of a number of organizations, in this particular case a referendum would be useful on one condition and that is that the subject would have to be simple, clear, and leave no room for any "ifs". The issue of nuclear power is very complex, and in my humble opinion,
very few Canadians would be able to evaluate the implications of a decision made simply by checking yes or no on a referendum slip. I would therefore like to take a few moments to elaborate.
Do Canadians realize that nuclear power is used in medical research to fight disease, to detect anomalies and to sterilize laboratory equipment? Do they know there is a process for preserving food by irradiation? Would people be able to consider all aspects of the issue if a referendum were held or even if a moratorium were imposed to give time to examine the question? Electing to stop research and development in the nuclear field would be tantamount to letting ourselves fall behind at the technological level and losing our position in an area where this country has now gained world recognition. Taking the risk of falling behind and losing our headstart is very risky indeed. Are people really well acquainted with the uses of nuclear power? It is clear, Mr. Speaker, that what we know best about nuclear power are its negative aspects. However, most Canadians know full well that our CANDU reactors are still in the forefront of nuclear technology. Mr. Speaker, 12 per cent of Canada's electricity is generated by nuclear power.
In Ontario, 85 per cent of the electricity is generated by nuclear power.
We should all recognize the value of the CANDU technology. Canada has developed a technologically advanced package that compares favourably on the international market. This remarkable achievement is the result of joint efforts by AECL, Ontario Hydro and other organizations. CANDU-produced electricity has an excellent safety, reliability and cost efficient record around the world.
In the summer of 1982, the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources released a federal study on nuclear industry. According to the study, long term prospects for Canadian nuclear industry are excellent.
I should like to remind my hon. friend that nuclear power is the cheapest source of electricity in many areas of this country. Is he against progress? Is he more conservative than we think? In spite of the current low demand, CANDU reactors remain interesting both on the Canadian and international markets. They have immediate spinoffs which should not be ignored.
Atomic Energy of Canada Ltd., a Crown corporation, is currently going through a transition period. It has suffered because of a decreased international demand for nuclear reactors which make sales difficult. It remains committed to marketing and development efforts of its main product, the CANDU reactor, to make it competitive with other types of reactors.
October 22, 1985

In 1984, revenue from supply and services decreased by 25 per cent, going down to SI46.3 million, mostly because of the few openings in the nuclear reactor market.
In spite of these problems, the CENARVODA project is going forward and Rumania announced a long-term program to build ten CAN DU 600 reactors by the year 2000.
The corporation has signed an agreement in principle with Turkey and is now putting together a comprehensive financing program for the approval of Cabinet. The corporation might also sell other products to Korea, Japan, Yugoslavia and Indonesia, where the AECL has now reached the last stages in its negotiations to supply a nuclear research laboratory.
Mr. Speaker, there is light at the end of the tunnel and we must continue to work together as we strive for it. I am certain that the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie) has no intention of taking away the bread from the workers in this sector.
It is to be hoped that this marketing problem will solve itself in 1985-86.
To support its commitment to more a business-like approach in financial management, the Government has been taking action to improve the administration of public funds. After assessing the role of the AECL in the nuclear field, and especially its research and development activities, the Government has concluded that the CANDU technology has made its mark and is now quite well-known. This is why it decided to reduce the funds allocated to this corporation in its budget of May 1985.
This reduction will take place over the next five years to bring down the amount allocated to the corporation from the present yearly level of about $200 million to $100 million by the end of the decade. However, the Government will continue to emphasize health and safety research programs since these involve the long-term interests of both the Canadian nuclear industry and the users of CANDU technology. The AECL will have to find other potential sources of financing, particularly from major users of the CANDU reactors, such as Ontario Hydro, to compensate for the loss of financing resources for research and development activities brought about by the reduction of the contribution made by the federal Government.
In its budget of May 1985, the Government also announced the closure of two heavy water plants operated by the AECL in Cape Breton Island since the country already has abundant heavy water supplies and there are other sources of production available to meet all foreseeable needs of the Canadian and foreign markets.
The closure of these facilities should save the Government over $100 million a year.

subtopic: TRANSPORT (A) NEED TO ESTABLISH A "BUY CANADIAN" POLICY. (B) PURCHASE OF
TRANSPORT (A) NEED TO ESTABLISH A "BUY CANADIAN" POLICY. (B) PURCHASE OF
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my duty tonight to remind the House of this Tory Government's failure to establish a "Buy Canadian" policy in Canada in the area of transportation.
Last week I directed a question on this subject to the Minister of State (Transport) (Mrs. Blais-Grenier), and I see she is in her place tonight to listen and, hopefully, to try and clarify the very vague answers she gave me last week. I wanted to know whether her Government had a "Buy Canadian" policy in the area of transportation.
Her answer was that she was looking at the situation in order to find out whether there was in fact substitution from Canadian production in Montreal to production abroad. What joke!
Mr. Speaker, there is no need for the Minister to look at the situation to realize and understand that many companies in Montreal East which are directly related to transportation are closing down. Bombardier closed down their locomotive plant, because they had no contracts from the Government of Canada.
The CN has laid off 474 employees due to the closing down of its maintenance centre in Montreal, because of the policies of this Conservative Government. The CSW Ironworks have laid off 130 workers, because the contract for 1,000 rolling stock wheels for CP Rail was awarded to a Brazilian company. And the CSF Foundry, the survival of which is directly dependent upon the federal Budget, has had to lay off more than 500 employees.
What more does the Minister need to end her endless studies and take action? All she has to do is open her eyes and see what is going on in her own and in neighbouring Montreal constituencies.
The president of the CSF Foundry Steelworkers Local Union, Mr. Antonio Pennestri, believes the Minister of State (Transport) lacks interest and is showing great indifference to workers' problems.
Let me quote him:
If the Minister fails to move and to award rail car construction contracts, what will become of us?

October 22, 1985
Adjournment Debate
-this is what Mr. Pennestri is saying. Those words clearly show the concern and the insecurity that company's workers have to face.
As supplementary, I also asked the Minister of State (Transport) whether she would contact the Canadian railways to ensure that they buy rolling stock wheels made in Canada rather than in Brazil. The Minister answered that she was examining this issue to find out exactly how pertinent that matter could be. That was her answer! Ridicule never killed anyone. "How pertinent that matter could be". What does that mean? The workers of the Steelworkers Union do not know what the Minister means. To them, "the pertinent matter" is that under a Liberal Government, they were working, there were contracts for those companies. But now that the Conservatives are in power, there are no contracts and those workers are losing their jobs.
What is quite unbelievable about those 130 people laid off in the CSW Ironworks is that apparently, the contract for 6,000 rolling stock wheels granted to Brazil would save about SI00 per wheel to Canadian Pacific. Six thousand wheels at $100 each amounts to about $600,000. Now, due to the Progressive Conservative Government's inaction, those 130 workers who have been laid off will get unemployment insurance for 52 weeks, at about $275 per week, totalling $14,000 for 130 people. It means that the Government of Canada will have to pay out about $1.8 million. Thus, CP will save $600,000 but the Government of Canada will have to pay three times that amount in unemployment insurance benefits.
That is why, Mr. Speaker, I find this situation quite ludicrous. The Minister must take action to ensure that from now on, Canadian railways buy their rolling stock in Canada. Otherwise, if the Conservative Government does not act, there will be more unemployed in this area and we will lose a vital sector of our rolling stock industry, which was established at the beginning of the century in the East End of Montreal, where a skilled and adequate labour force is there to do the job provided they get some help from the Government.
I hope that the Minister who has listened to me will finally take on her responsibilities and find some contracts to bring those people back to work as soon as possible.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for his interest-rather sudden, I must admit-in the workers of Montreal East. I will not comment on what might motivate him.
He seems to be blaming me for taking time to study a rather complex file involving such major railway companies as CN and CP. I met with CSW union president Antoine Pennestri who asked me a series of questions. I told him I would have answers to his questions within ten days, and I will have answers to Mr. Pennestri's questions within ten days.
Here is the latest update on this file. In 1984 the Canadian Government placed an order for 2,460 cars, the total amount of new railway cars for 1984 and 1985.
Projected hopper-car requirements are revised in November each year, but the current situation is somewhat special, in the sense that neither CN or CP, I am told, want to make predictions about the number of cars they will need, simply because the volume of rail freight has nosedived this year and railway companies do not expect it to go up again before two years. They are facing drastic cuts in coal, potash and wheat shipping, and their income has decreased accordingly.
In addition, CN and CP are still improving their rolling stock turn-around cycles, so they are making more special arrangements to avoid return trips with empty cars, thus resulting in greater efficiency and a better use of their rolling stock, and consequently a net decrease in the need to acquire new equipment.
With a net decrease in grain production and demand there seems to be no need for the railroads to increase their car capacity. Moreover they can make their own cars, as has been the case with the CN over the last few years. In doing so the CN now competes with production of hopper cars with companies such as CSW since CN can direct and determine its own production according to its needs.
Of course there are exceptions to that situation. In 1984 for example, CN was able to buy cars on a long term lease arrangement. This was very profitable for the company because it did not translate into an annual debt.
However, under that long term lease arrangement, the CN bought 1,600 hopper cars, which after only five years of use were still in top shape and at a unit price of only $20,000, as compared to the market price of $60,000 for new cars. Obviously, nobody would blame the company for trying to lower its deficit and do it in the most effective way possible by optimizing the use of its rolling stock.
On the other hand CP admits buying wheels from the Mafersa company in Brazil. According to CP, and this is something I was not aware of and I am trying to have it further investigated, the tests on those wheels proved very conclusive in view of the fact that according to CP they are of a higher quality and longer-lasting. We are obviously dealing with companies that have to be very competitive on the market place and which must do whatever they possibly can to remain so.

subtopic: BANKS AND BANKING-MINISTER'S LETTER TO SHAREHOLDER. (B) POSITION OF SHAREHOLDERS
BANKS AND BANKING-MINISTER'S LETTER TO SHAREHOLDER. (B) POSITION OF SHAREHOLDERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on October 10, I asked two questions of the Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDougall) concerning assurances she had given in a letter of August 9 to a worried shareholder of the Canadian
October 22, 1985

Commercial Bank. In that letter she assured the shareholder that the CCB was viable and could be expected to be profitable. If the shareholder had sold his shares at that point he might have received approximately $5 for each one he held. He had originally paid $25 for each one. However, on the basis of the Minister's assurances he held on to his shares and on September 1 the Canadian Commercial Bank closed its doors. This man found he had lost everything. He is not a particularly rich man. The money he had used to buy these shares was part of his retirement planning. He is a farmer who had begun to sell off some of his assets as he tried to relieve himself of some of the hard work of farming in preparation for his retirement.
I also have a letter from a 70-year old man, who is not rich either, who sold his home and was strongly advised that the Canadian Commercial Bank was a good place for him to put his money. He was told it would be a safe investment. He, too, by September 1 had lost everything.
I talked to a widow today who had $5,000 in shares in the Canadian Commercial Bank. This is not a large amount of money to everyone but it is a large amount to her. That money is now gone.
Closure was moved on a Bill which was before the House with respect to reimbursing uninsured depositors. These are depositors who, in any case, will receive up to $60,000 from the Canadian Deposit Insurance Corporation. A person with more than one account in the bank, perhaps a current account and a registered plan of some type, may receive more than $60,000. The Government is then moving to reimburse them fully for the difference between what the CDIC will pay and the amount of their total deposit.
Apparently, the Government is taking that stand because of statements made between March 25 and September 1, when Government officials made many, many public declarations that the Canadian Commercial Bank was safe, secure, viable and would be profitable in the future. March 25 was the date the Government arranged a bail-out for the bank and injected some $255 million into it. September 1, of course, is the date the bank closed its doors. The Government has, therefore, taken the line that there is some kind of moral obligation created by the statements to pay out all depositors in full. But the Government is not taking the same position with respect to the debenture holders or the preferred shareholders.
My Party takes the position that any moral obligation there may be to pay out uninsured depositors-and perhaps it is a little grandiose to call it a moral obligation-was created by Government incompetence and should not be be binding on the taxpayers of this country. We would not be opposed to setting up some kind of hardship fund for which people could apply, but it seems that some of the shareholders might have just as much claim on a hardship fund as some of the depositors.
The banks who participated in the bail-out on March 25 are also taking the position that if the Government has a moral obligation to depositors, it has the same moral obligation to the
Adjournment Debate
banks. We must remember that this is a wholesale bank so the depositors are not, by and large, small individual accounts. The depositors are businesses. And while the breakdown we have been given of categories of deposits shows some individuals, it also shows at least two individuals in for very large amounts-in the nature of $1 million. So we are not generally talking about very poor depositors. We are talking about a lot of commercial paper. And some of the banks are taking the position that the Government by its statements has created an obligation to depositors, therefore there is a similar obligation to the banks who participated in the bail-out.
The banks asked for, as a condition of their bail-out, a letter saying that the bail-out would make the Canadian Commercial Bank viable. They received such a letter dated April 26, signed by the Inspector General of Banks. Between the time of the bail-out and April 26 the banks had been pressuring the Government to do a closer examination of the situation of the Canadian Commercial Bank.
The Bank's original request to have this done on the weekend of March 22-25 was refused. Nothing happened before April 26 when they received the letter saying that the Canadian Commercial Bank was viable. Again, this was a letter clearly based to a large extent on faith. At some point after April 26 a more serious look was taken at the assets of the Canadian Commercial Bank. At the end of June, Mr. Hitch-man was appointed and we know the results. Therefore, 1 would ask the Government to explain what responsibility it is prepared to undertake for its many misleading statements, not only to depositors but to shareholders and to the participants in the bail-out?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: BANKS AND BANKING-MINISTER'S LETTER TO SHAREHOLDER. (B) POSITION OF SHAREHOLDERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to rise and answer the question raised by the Hon. Member for Trinity (Miss Nicholson) concerning our Government's decision not to reimburse ordinary Canadian Commercial Bank and Northland Bank shareholders.
The Members of this noble institution are aware that Bill C-79, which was finally adopted this afternoon, will provide adequate compensation for the regular depositors of the banks that went bankrupt. As the Minister of State (Finance) (Mrs. McDougall) told the House, the Government feels it would be unfair if the depositors who left their money with the banks, thus contributing to efforts made to keep the two financial institutions on an even keel, were to see their money go up in smoke, whereas others who withdrew their deposits during the summer got all their money back, under quite similar conditions.
Our Government is prepared to compensate the depositors of the institutions that went bankrupt. However it does not intend to extend that support to other categories of investors, that is creditors and ordinary investors, including the debenture holders and shareholders of those banks. Investors should know that debentures and ordinary shares involve a higher inherent

October 22, 1985
Adjournment Debate
risk than simple deposits. Prior rank investors who bought bank debentures did so in the hope of getting higher interest than those granted to ordinary depositors. In return for this higher yield, the holders of those debentures voluntarily assumed part of the risks that come with any commercial undertaking.
Other junior rank investors who bought shares of those banks, in order to participate without limit in the profits of those two institutions, rank equally. They acted in the hope of getting a higher after-tax yield than that given to the depositors of those banks. Shareholders of any private commercial venture, be it a bank or a small business, must be willing to accept the risk of a bankruptcy in compensation for higher gains they would have pocketed if the business had done well.
